turn_logs.content: I began my illustrious career in journalism in the Bronx where I toiled as a hard-boiled reporter for the Ram, the student newspaper at Fordham University. And one day I'm walking toward the campus center and out comes the elusive Dean McGowan, architect of a policy to replace Fordham's traditionally working- to middle-class students with wealthier, more prestigious ones. So I whip out my notebook and I go up to him and I say, "Dean McGowan, is it true that Fordham University plans to raise tuition substantially above the inflation rate, and if so, wouldn't that be a betrayal of its mission?" And he stops and looks at me and he says, "Listen up, punk." And right then, there's a blur in the corner of my eye which becomes this figure holding a cream pie which becomes the guy standing next to me mashing a cream pie into Dean McGowan's face. And then runs away. And the Dean is covered with cream. So I give him a moment, and then I say, "Dean McGowan, would you care to comment on this latest attack?" And the Dean says, "Yes, I would care to comment. Fuck you." So I race back to the newsroom with my scoop and I find the editor, Jim Dwyer, who's a senior, and he will go on to win a Pulitzer Prize, that is true, and he's a big guy. I pitch him my story, I tell him what I've seen, and he says, "Dean McGowan, that guy's a dick. Write it up." So I'm banging out my story and I know it's good, and then I start to make it better, by adding an element of embellishment. Reporters call this "making shit up." And they recommend against crossing that line. But I had just seen the line crossed between a high-powered dean and assault with a pastry, and I kind of liked it. So the first I did was I gave the figure a name. I called him "Pie Man," capital "P," capital "M." And I described him as a cape-wearing, masked avenger. Though in fact he'd been capeless. And said that as he fled the scene, he clicked his heels in rakish glee. And I gave him a catchphrase in Latin. I said that he cried out, "Ego sum non an bestia," which means "I am not an animal." Which makes no sense. I needed something. I'm Catholic, Latin just comes to me. So I finish my story and I hand it to Dwyer, and he reads and he says, "Pie Man? I love it. Page one." And that's how the first line got crossed. A few days later, I get a letter. It says, "Dear Jim, good story. Nice details. If you want to see me again in action, be on the steps of Duane Library Tuesday at 3 o'clock," signed Pie Man. So I was there with a photographer from the Ram. And sure enough, out comes Sheila Beale, student-body president. And now Sheila was different from me and all the other Fordham students who wore flannel shirts and worked part-time jobs. Sheila was well-bred. Sheila had school spirit. Sheila was the kind of student that Dean McGown wanted more of. Although rumor had it that he got plenty of her in his office on his desk. But that's just a rumor, please do not spread it outside this rumor. I myself would never say that. But the fact was, Sheila had collaborated with the Dean to ban outdoor drinking on campus. The infamous "no more beer at barbecues" rule. That's right, boo that rule. Sheila thought drinking in public was in poor taste. I think you know what happened next. Pie Man emerged from behind the late-night library drop-box, made his delivery, and fled away, crying, "Ego sum non an bestia." Or at least that's what it said in my story in the newspaper the next day, which ran with a photo of him leaving the scene, cape flowing behind him, doing this. And that's what made him a sensation on campus. People started dressing like him and quoting him in class. The Ram ran five major stories about Pie Man, all of them by me. And toward the end of this run, I was out at a bar one night, and I saw, I came and I saw in the corner Angela from my Brit Lit class, drinking with some friends. And now Angela and I had been flirting for two months. Or I had been flirting with her, and with such nuance that there was a question about whether she knew I existed. So I, I saw her there and made a mental note to do nothing about it. And then I went to the bar to buy a round and I felt a tap on my shoulder. And it was her. And she said, "Jim, we were just talking about how you always seem to know when and where Pie Man will strike. And we were wondering, are you Pie Man?" And I knew by the way she said it, I knew that if I said yes, she would have sex with me. And wasn't I really Pie Man? For having brought him into being. Didn't she only know about him through me? But she had asked me a straightforward question that came with a straightforward answer. In fact, I wasn't Pie Man. As far as I knew, I had never seen the guy out of costume. So I looked at her and I said, "Yes, Angela. I am Pie Man." And she said, "Oh, good. Now buy me a beer and tell me all about it."

turn_logs.content: I began my illustrious career in journalism in the Bronx where I toiled as a hard-boiled reporter for the Ram, the student newspaper at Fordham University. And one day I'm walking toward the campus center and out comes the elusive Dean McGowan, architect of a policy to replace Fordham's traditionally working- to middle-class students with wealthier, more prestigious ones. So I whip out my notebook and I go up to him and I say, "Dean McGowan, is it true that Fordham University plans to raise tuition substantially above the inflation rate, and if so, wouldn't that be a betrayal of its mission?" And he stops and looks at me and he says, "Listen up, punk." And right then, there's a blur in the corner of my eye which becomes this figure holding a cream pie which becomes the guy standing next to me mashing a cream pie into Dean McGowan's face. And then runs away. And the Dean is covered with cream. So I give him a moment, and then I say, "Dean McGowan, would you care to comment on this latest attack?" And the Dean says, "Yes, I would care to comment. Fuck you." So I race back to the newsroom with my scoop and I find the editor, Jim Dwyer, who's a senior, and he will go on to win a Pulitzer Prize, that is true, and he's a big guy. I pitch him my story, I tell him what I've seen, and he says, "Dean McGowan, that guy's a dick. Write it up." So I'm banging out my story and I know it's good, and then I start to make it better, by adding an element of embellishment. Reporters call this "making shit up." And they recommend against crossing that line. But I had just seen the line crossed between a high-powered dean and assault with a pastry, and I kind of liked it. So the first I did was I gave the figure a name. I called him "Pie Man," capital "P," capital "M." And I described him as a cape-wearing, masked avenger. Though in fact he'd been capeless. And said that as he fled the scene, he clicked his heels in rakish glee. And I gave him a catchphrase in Latin. I said that he cried out, "Ego sum non an bestia," which means "I am not an animal." Which makes no sense. I needed something. I'm Catholic, Latin just comes to me. So I finish my story and I hand it to Dwyer, and he reads and he says, "Pie Man? I love it. Page one." And that's how the first line got crossed. A few days later, I get a letter. It says, "Dear Jim, good story. Nice details. If you want to see me again in action, be on the steps of Duane Library Tuesday at 3 o'clock," signed Pie Man. So I was there with a photographer from the Ram. And sure enough, out comes Sheila Beale, student-body president. And now Sheila was different from me and all the other Fordham students who wore flannel shirts and worked part-time jobs. Sheila was well-bred. Sheila had school spirit. Sheila was the kind of student that Dean McGown wanted more of. Although rumor had it that he got plenty of her in his office on his desk. But that's just a rumor, please do not spread it outside this rumor. I myself would never say that. But the fact was, Sheila had collaborated with the Dean to ban outdoor drinking on campus. The infamous "no more beer at barbecues" rule. That's right, boo that rule. Sheila thought drinking in public was in poor taste. I think you know what happened next. Pie Man emerged from behind the late-night library drop-box, made his delivery, and fled away, crying, "Ego sum non an bestia." Or at least that's what it said in my story in the newspaper the next day, which ran with a photo of him leaving the scene, cape flowing behind him, doing this. And that's what made him a sensation on campus. People started dressing like him and quoting him in class. The Ram ran five major stories about Pie Man, all of them by me. And toward the end of this run, I was out at a bar one night, and I saw, I came and I saw in the corner Angela from my Brit Lit class, drinking with some friends. And now Angela and I had been flirting for two months. Or I had been flirting with her, and with such nuance that there was a question about whether she knew I existed. So I, I saw her there and made a mental note to do nothing about it. And then I went to the bar to buy a round and I felt a tap on my shoulder. And it was her. And she said, "Jim, we were just talking about how you always seem to know when and where Pie Man will strike. And we were wondering, are you Pie Man?" And I knew by the way she said it, I knew that if I said yes, she would have sex with me. And wasn't I really Pie Man? For having brought him into being. Didn't she only know about him through me? But she had asked me a straightforward question that came with a straightforward answer. In fact, I wasn't Pie Man. As far as I knew, I had never seen the guy out of costume. So I looked at her and I said, "Yes, Angela. I am Pie Man." And she said, "Oh, good. Now buy me a beer and tell me all about it."

And one day I'm walking toward the campus center and out comes the elusive Dean McGowan, architect of a policy to replace Fordham's traditionally working- to middle-class students with wealthier, more prestigious ones. So I whip out my notebook and I go up to him and I say, "Dean McGowan, is it true that Fordham University plans to raise tuition substantially above the inflation rate, and if so, wouldn't that be a betrayal of its mission?" And he stops and looks at me and he says, "Listen up, punk." And right then, there's a blur in the corner of my eye which becomes this figure holding a cream pie which becomes the guy standing next to me mashing a cream pie into Dean McGowan's face. And then runs away. And the Dean is covered with cream. So I give him a moment, and then I say, "Dean McGowan, would you care to comment on this latest attack?" And the Dean says, "Yes, I would care to comment. Fuck you." So I race back to the newsroom with my scoop and I find the editor, Jim Dwyer, who's a senior, and he will go on to win a Pulitzer Prize, that is true, and he's a big guy. I pitch him my story, I tell him what I've seen, and he says, "Dean McGowan, that guy's a dick. Write it up." So I'm banging out my story and I know it's good, and then I start to make it better, by adding an element of embellishment. Reporters call this "making shit up." And they recommend against crossing that line. But I had just seen the line crossed between a high-powered dean and assault with a pastry, and I kind of liked it. So the first I did was I gave the figure a name. I called him "Pie Man," capital "P," capital "M." And I described him as a cape-wearing, masked avenger. Though in fact he'd been capeless. And said that as he fled the scene, he clicked his heels in rakish glee. And I gave him a catchphrase in Latin. I said that he cried out, "Ego sum non an bestia," which means "I am not an animal." Which makes no sense. I needed something. I'm Catholic, Latin just comes to me. So I finish my story and I hand it to Dwyer, and he reads and he says, "Pie Man? I love it. Page one." And that's how the first line got crossed. A few days later, I get a letter. It says, "Dear Jim, good story. Nice details. If you want to see me again in action, be on the steps of Duane Library Tuesday at 3 o'clock," signed Pie Man. So I was there with a photographer from the Ram. And sure enough, out comes Sheila Beale, student-body president. And now Sheila was different from me and all the other Fordham students who wore flannel shirts and worked part-time jobs. Sheila was well-bred. Sheila had school spirit. Sheila was the kind of student that Dean McGown wanted more of. Although rumor had it that he got plenty of her in his office on his desk. But that's just a rumor, please do not spread it outside this rumor. I myself would never say that. But the fact was, Sheila had collaborated with the Dean to ban outdoor drinking on campus. The infamous "no more beer at barbecues" rule. That's right, boo that rule. Sheila thought drinking in public was in poor taste. I think you know what happened next. Pie Man emerged from behind the late-night library drop-box, made his delivery, and fled away, crying, "Ego sum non an bestia." Or at least that's what it said in my story in the newspaper the next day, which ran with a photo of him leaving the scene, cape flowing behind him, doing this. And that's what made him a sensation on campus. People started dressing like him and quoting him in class. The Ram ran five major stories about Pie Man, all of them by me. And toward the end of this run, I was out at a bar one night, and I saw, I came and I saw in the corner Angela from my Brit Lit class, drinking with some friends. And now Angela and I had been flirting for two months. Or I had been flirting with her, and with such nuance that there was a question about whether she knew I existed. So I, I saw her there and made a mental note to do nothing about it. And then I went to the bar to buy a round and I felt a tap on my shoulder. And it was her. And she said, "Jim, we were just talking about how you always seem to know when and where Pie Man will strike. And we were wondering, are you Pie Man?" And I knew by the way she said it, I knew that if I said yes, she would have sex with me. And wasn't I really Pie Man? For having brought him into being. Didn't she only know about him through me? But she had asked me a straightforward question that came with a straightforward answer. In fact, I wasn't Pie Man. As far as I knew, I had never seen the guy out of costume. So I looked at her and I said, "Yes, Angela. I am Pie Man." And she said, "Oh, good. Now buy me a beer and tell me all about it."

turn_logs.content: I began my illustrious career in journalism in the Bronx where I toiled as a hard-boiled reporter for the Ram, the student newspaper at Fordham University. And one day I'm walking toward the campus center and out comes the elusive Dean McGowan, architect of a policy to replace Fordham's traditionally working- to middle-class students with wealthier, more prestigious ones. So I whip out my notebook and I go up to him and I say, "Dean McGowan, is it true that Fordham University plans to raise tuition substantially above the inflation rate, and if so, wouldn't that be a betrayal of its mission?" And he stops and looks at me and he says, "Listen up, punk." And right then, there's a blur in the corner of my eye which becomes this figure holding a cream pie which becomes the guy standing next to me mashing a cream pie into Dean McGowan's face. And then runs away. And the Dean is covered with cream. So I give him a moment, and then I say, "Dean McGowan, would you care to comment on this latest attack?" And the Dean says, "Yes, I would care to comment. Fuck you." So I race back to the newsroom with my scoop and I find the editor, Jim Dwyer, who's a senior, and he will go on to win a Pulitzer Prize, that is true, and he's a big guy. I pitch him my story, I tell him what I've seen, and he says, "Dean McGowan, that guy's a dick. Write it up." So I'm banging out my story and I know it's good, and then I start to make it better, by adding an element of embellishment. Reporters call this "making shit up." And they recommend against crossing that line. But I had just seen the line crossed between a high-powered dean and assault with a pastry, and I kind of liked it. So the first I did was I gave the figure a name. I called him "Pie Man," capital "P," capital "M." And I described him as a cape-wearing, masked avenger. Though in fact he'd been capeless. And said that as he fled the scene, he clicked his heels in rakish glee. And I gave him a catchphrase in Latin. I said that he cried out, "Ego sum non an bestia," which means "I am not an animal." Which makes no sense. I needed something. I'm Catholic, Latin just comes to me. So I finish my story and I hand it to Dwyer, and he reads and he says, "Pie Man? I love it. Page one." And that's how the first line got crossed. A few days later, I get a letter. It says, "Dear Jim, good story. Nice details. If you want to see me again in action, be on the steps of Duane Library Tuesday at 3 o'clock," signed Pie Man. So I was there with a photographer from the Ram. And sure enough, out comes Sheila Beale, student-body president. And now Sheila was different from me and all the other Fordham students who wore flannel shirts and worked part-time jobs. Sheila was well-bred. Sheila had school spirit. Sheila was the kind of student that Dean McGown wanted more of. Although rumor had it that he got plenty of her in his office on his desk. But that's just a rumor, please do not spread it outside this rumor. I myself would never say that. But the fact was, Sheila had collaborated with the Dean to ban outdoor drinking on campus. The infamous "no more beer at barbecues" rule. That's right, boo that rule. Sheila thought drinking in public was in poor taste. I think you know what happened next. Pie Man emerged from behind the late-night library drop-box, made his delivery, and fled away, crying, "Ego sum non an bestia." Or at least that's what it said in my story in the newspaper the next day, which ran with a photo of him leaving the scene, cape flowing behind him, doing this. And that's what made him a sensation on campus. People started dressing like him and quoting him in class. The Ram ran five major stories about Pie Man, all of them by me. And toward the end of this run, I was out at a bar one night, and I saw, I came and I saw in the corner Angela from my Brit Lit class, drinking with some friends. And now Angela and I had been flirting for two months. Or I had been flirting with her, and with such nuance that there was a question about whether she knew I existed. So I, I saw her there and made a mental note to do nothing about it. And then I went to the bar to buy a round and I felt a tap on my shoulder. And it was her. And she said, "Jim, we were just talking about how you always seem to know when and where Pie Man will strike. And we were wondering, are you Pie Man?" And I knew by the way she said it, I knew that if I said yes, she would have sex with me. And wasn't I really Pie Man? For having brought him into being. Didn't she only know about him through me? But she had asked me a straightforward question that came with a straightforward answer. In fact, I wasn't Pie Man. As far as I knew, I had never seen the guy out of costume. So I looked at her and I said, "Yes, Angela. I am Pie Man." And she said, "Oh, good. Now buy me a beer and tell me all about it."

turn_logs.content: I began my illustrious career in journalism in the Bronx where I toiled as a hard-boiled reporter for the Ram, the student newspaper at Fordham University. And one day I'm walking toward the campus center and out comes the elusive Dean McGowan, architect of a policy to replace Fordham's traditionally working- to middle-class students with wealthier, more prestigious ones. So I whip out my notebook and I go up to him and I say, "Dean McGowan, is it true that Fordham University plans to raise tuition substantially above the inflation rate, and if so, wouldn't that be a betrayal of its mission?" And he stops and looks at me and he says, "Listen up, punk." And right then, there's a blur in the corner of my eye which becomes this figure holding a cream pie which becomes the guy standing next to me mashing a cream pie into Dean McGowan's face. And then runs away. And the Dean is covered with cream. So I give him a moment, and then I say, "Dean McGowan, would you care to comment on this latest attack?" And the Dean says, "Yes, I would care to comment. Fuck you." So I race back to the newsroom with my scoop and I find the editor, Jim Dwyer, who's a senior, and he will go on to win a Pulitzer Prize, that is true, and he's a big guy. I pitch him my story, I tell him what I've seen, and he says, "Dean McGowan, that guy's a dick. Write it up." So I'm banging out my story and I know it's good, and then I start to make it better, by adding an element of embellishment. Reporters call this "making shit up." And they recommend against crossing that line. But I had just seen the line crossed between a high-powered dean and assault with a pastry, and I kind of liked it. So the first I did was I gave the figure a name. I called him "Pie Man," capital "P," capital "M." And I described him as a cape-wearing, masked avenger. Though in fact he'd been capeless. And said that as he fled the scene, he clicked his heels in rakish glee. And I gave him a catchphrase in Latin. I said that he cried out, "Ego sum non an bestia," which means "I am not an animal." Which makes no sense. I needed something. I'm Catholic, Latin just comes to me. So I finish my story and I hand it to Dwyer, and he reads and he says, "Pie Man? I love it. Page one." And that's how the first line got crossed. A few days later, I get a letter. It says, "Dear Jim, good story. Nice details. If you want to see me again in action, be on the steps of Duane Library Tuesday at 3 o'clock," signed Pie Man. So I was there with a photographer from the Ram. And sure enough, out comes Sheila Beale, student-body president. And now Sheila was different from me and all the other Fordham students who wore flannel shirts and worked part-time jobs. Sheila was well-bred. Sheila had school spirit. Sheila was the kind of student that Dean McGown wanted more of. Although rumor had it that he got plenty of her in his office on his desk. But that's just a rumor, please do not spread it outside this rumor. I myself would never say that. But the fact was, Sheila had collaborated with the Dean to ban outdoor drinking on campus. The infamous "no more beer at barbecues" rule. That's right, boo that rule. Sheila thought drinking in public was in poor taste. I think you know what happened next. Pie Man emerged from behind the late-night library drop-box, made his delivery, and fled away, crying, "Ego sum non an bestia." Or at least that's what it said in my story in the newspaper the next day, which ran with a photo of him leaving the scene, cape flowing behind him, doing this. And that's what made him a sensation on campus. People started dressing like him and quoting him in class. The Ram ran five major stories about Pie Man, all of them by me. And toward the end of this run, I was out at a bar one night, and I saw, I came and I saw in the corner Angela from my Brit Lit class, drinking with some friends. And now Angela and I had been flirting for two months. Or I had been flirting with her, and with such nuance that there was a question about whether she knew I existed. So I, I saw her there and made a mental note to do nothing about it. And then I went to the bar to buy a round and I felt a tap on my shoulder. And it was her. And she said, "Jim, we were just talking about how you always seem to know when and where Pie Man will strike. And we were wondering, are you Pie Man?" And I knew by the way she said it, I knew that if I said yes, she would have sex with me. And wasn't I really Pie Man? For having brought him into being. Didn't she only know about him through me? But she had asked me a straightforward question that came with a straightforward answer. In fact, I wasn't Pie Man. As far as I knew, I had never seen the guy out of costume. So I looked at her and I said, "Yes, Angela. I am Pie Man." And she said, "Oh, good. Now buy me a beer and tell me all about it."

And one day I'm walking toward the campus center and out comes the elusive Dean McGowan, architect of a policy to replace Fordham's traditionally working- to middle-class students with wealthier, more prestigious ones. So I whip out my notebook and I go up to him and I say, "Dean McGowan, is it true that Fordham University plans to raise tuition substantially above the inflation rate, and if so, wouldn't that be a betrayal of its mission?" And he stops and looks at me and he says, "Listen up, punk." And right then, there's a blur in the corner of my eye which becomes this figure holding a cream pie which becomes the guy standing next to me mashing a cream pie into Dean McGowan's face. And then runs away. And the Dean is covered with cream. So I give him a moment, and then I say, "Dean McGowan, would you care to comment on this latest attack?" And the Dean says, "Yes, I would care to comment. Fuck you." So I race back to the newsroom with my scoop and I find the editor, Jim Dwyer, who's a senior, and he will go on to win a Pulitzer Prize, that is true, and he's a big guy. I pitch him my story, I tell him what I've seen, and he says, "Dean McGowan, that guy's a dick. Write it up." So I'm banging out my story and I know it's good, and then I start to make it better, by adding an element of embellishment. Reporters call this "making shit up." And they recommend against crossing that line. But I had just seen the line crossed between a high-powered dean and assault with a pastry, and I kind of liked it. So the first I did was I gave the figure a name. I called him "Pie Man," capital "P," capital "M." And I described him as a cape-wearing, masked avenger. Though in fact he'd been capeless. And said that as he fled the scene, he clicked his heels in rakish glee. And I gave him a catchphrase in Latin. I said that he cried out, "Ego sum non an bestia," which means "I am not an animal." Which makes no sense. I needed something. I'm Catholic, Latin just comes to me. So I finish my story and I hand it to Dwyer, and he reads and he says, "Pie Man? I love it. Page one." And that's how the first line got crossed. A few days later, I get a letter. It says, "Dear Jim, good story. Nice details. If you want to see me again in action, be on the steps of Duane Library Tuesday at 3 o'clock," signed Pie Man. So I was there with a photographer from the Ram. And sure enough, out comes Sheila Beale, student-body president. And now Sheila was different from me and all the other Fordham students who wore flannel shirts and worked part-time jobs. Sheila was well-bred. Sheila had school spirit. Sheila was the kind of student that Dean McGown wanted more of. Although rumor had it that he got plenty of her in his office on his desk. But that's just a rumor, please do not spread it outside this rumor. I myself would never say that. But the fact was, Sheila had collaborated with the Dean to ban outdoor drinking on campus. And toward the end of this run, I was out at a bar one night, and I saw, I came and I saw in the corner Angela from my Brit Lit class, drinking with some friends. And now Angela and I had been flirting for two months. Or I had been flirting with her, and with such nuance that there was a question about whether she knew I existed. So I, I saw her there and made a mental note to do nothing about it. And then I went to the bar to buy a round and I felt a tap on my shoulder. And it was her. recall_text:
I was teaching third grade, and the last unit of the year was the Oregon Trail. Usually I liked goofy, immersive games with silly characters or bands, but with this unit I wanted it to feel serious and real, even though it was complicated for nine-year-olds.

I created an Oregon Trail simulation. The students became pioneers and got the names of real people who had died. They chose occupations from the 1840s. We did a forty-block walk through Manhattan so they could feel what the journey was like. Then we played a chance-based game that was part Oregon Trail video game and part Dungeons & Dragons with dice.

I dressed in a bonnet as Mary, the wagon train captain, and I hinted that someone might die. The class became obsessed with the danger. There was a snake oil salesman episode that made them “throw up,” and they loved it. After that they kept asking every day if someone was going to die.

In the Rockies, a wagon overturned and Katherine Chubbuck, Katie, was trapped. She got an infection and it got worse, and it became a near-death crisis. Dr. Ellis Chapman saved her. The only way she would die was on a six, and Katie rolled a three. The class erupted, and afterward Katie kept saying that she almost died.

recall_text:
The narrator is a teacher teaching third grade, and the last unit of the year is the Oregon Trail. Usually the teacher does goofy immersive games with silly names and letters, but wanted this unit to feel serious and real even though the kids were nine.

The teacher made an Oregon Trail simulation. The students took the names of real people who died. They chose occupations from the 1840s. They also took a 40-block walk through Manhattan so they could feel how long the journey was. Then they played a chance game that mixed the Oregon Trail video game with Dungeons & Dragons dice.

One student, Alex Bacon, kept asking if it was dangerous and if someone could die. The teacher said yes because she wanted to raise the stakes, even though she did not actually intend for anyone to die. The class got really excited by the danger.

Near the end, Katie, or Katherine, Chubbuck was almost killed in a wagon accident. Her legs were infected, but Dr. Ellis Chapman saved her on a roll of three. After that, the teacher took away the danger and gave the class a baby wolf named Yenny the Benny. They got to Oregon quickly after that and celebrated with cornbread and a dance party to “September.” Years later, Katie still remembered almost dying.

I was teaching third grade, and the last unit of the year was the Oregon Trail. Usually I liked to make my lessons goofy and immersive, with silly names and fake letters and games, but for this unit I wanted it to feel serious and real, even though the kids were only nine.

I made an Oregon Trail simulation. The students took the names of real people who had died on the trail, chose occupations from the 1840s, and did a forty-block walk through Manhattan so they could feel how long the journey was. Then we played a chance game that was part Oregon Trail video game and part Dungeons & Dragons, with dice.

I wore a bonnet and was Mary, the captain of the wagon train, and I told them that someone might die. They became fixated on the danger. They loved the setbacks, including some kind of snake-oil elixir that made them throw up, and they kept asking whether someone was going to die.

At one point Katie, or Katherine, Chubbuck was almost killed under a wagon and her legs were infected. Dr. Ellis Chapman saved her on a roll of three. After that I tried to steer away from the danger by giving them a baby wolf named Yenny the Benny. They got to Oregon quickly after that, and we celebrated with cornbread and a dance to “September.”

Years later, Katie was the first one to say to me, “Do you remember when I almost died on the Oregon Trail?” and I said yes.

recall_text:
I am a third-grade teacher, and the last unit of the year is the Oregon Trail. Usually I do goofy immersive games with silly characters and letters, but this time I wanted it to feel serious and real, even though the kids were only nine.

I created an Oregon Trail simulation. The students took the names of real people who died on the trail, chose 1840s occupations, took a 40-block walk through Manhattan to feel what the journey was like, and then played a chance game that was a mix of the Oregon Trail video game and Dungeons & Dragons dice.

A smart-aleck kid named Alex asked if it was a game and if they could die. I said it was a dangerous game and maybe someone might die. That made the class excited, and they came in eager every day.

At one point a snake oil salesman made them lose a day, but the kids loved it. Later Katherine Chubbuck was almost killed under a wagon, and Dr. Ellis Chapman saved her on a roll of three. The class celebrated wildly.

After that I took the danger out of it. I gave them a baby wolf named Yenny the Benny, and they got to Oregon quickly. They made cornbread and danced to “September.” A year later, Katie still remembered almost dying on the Oregon Trail.

recall_text:
I’m a third grade teacher, and the last unit we do is the Oregon Trail. Usually I make everything into some goofy immersive game with silly characters and letters, but with the Oregon Trail I wanted it to feel serious and real, even though the kids were only nine.

So I made this whole Oregon Trail simulation. The students took the names of real people who had died on the trail, and they chose occupations from the 1840s. We did a forty-block walk through Manhattan so they could feel how long and hard the journey was. Then we played a game that was partly the Oregon Trail computer game and partly Dungeons & Dragons, with chance and dice rolls deciding what happened.

I dressed up in a bonnet as Mary, the captain of the wagon train, and I told them that someone might die. The kids got completely obsessed with the danger. At one point there was a snake oil salesman episode that made them throw up for a day, and they loved it.

The biggest thing I remember is Katie, or Katherine Chubbuck, almost dying. She was nearly killed under a wagon and her legs got infected, but Dr. Ellis Chapman saved her on a roll of three. After that I backed off from the danger and made things gentler. I gave them a baby wolf named Yenny the Benny, we got to Oregon quickly, and then we made cornbread and danced to “September.” Years later, Katie still remembered almost dying on the Oregon Trail.

recall_text:
A teacher narrates teaching third grade, and the last unit is the Oregon Trail. Usually the teacher does goofy immersive games with silly characters or bands, but wanted this one to feel serious and real even though the kids were nine.

The teacher created an Oregon Trail roleplay or simulation. The students took the names of real people who died, chose 1840s jobs, and took a 40-block walk in Manhattan to feel the journey. Then they made choices and rolled dice, like the Oregon Trail video game mixed with Dungeons & Dragons.

One student, Alex Bacon, kept asking if someone could die. The teacher, dressed in a bonnet as Mary, the wagon train captain, said yes, even though privately the teacher planned that no one would die. The class got excited by the danger and asked every day if someone would die.

At one point a snake oil salesman made them lose a day throwing up. Later Katherine Chubbuck was nearly killed under a wagon with infected legs, but Dr. Ellis Chapman saved her on a roll of 3. After that the teacher took away the danger and gave them a baby wolf named Yenny the Benny. They reached Oregon quickly, made cornbread, and danced to “September.” Years later Katie remembered “when I almost died on the Oregon Trail.”

The teacher made an Oregon Trail simulation. The students took the names of real people who died, chose 1840s occupations, took a 40-block walk in Manhattan to feel what the journey was like, and then played a chance game that mixed the Oregon Trail video game with Dungeons & Dragons dice.

A student named Alex asked if it was a game and if they could die. The teacher said it was a dangerous game and that someone might die, even though the teacher did not actually intend for there to be real in-game death. After that, the kids became obsessed with the danger and kept asking every day if someone was going to die.

Near the end, Katie, or Katherine Chubbuck, was almost killed when a wagon overturned and an infection got worse, but Dr. Ellis Chapman saved her on a roll of 3, and everyone celebrated. After that the teacher took the danger out of it, gave them a baby wolf named Yenny the Benny, and they got to Oregon quickly, made cornbread, and danced to “September.”

Years later, Katie remembered it and said, “Do you remember when I almost died on the Oregon Trail?” and the teacher said yes.

recall_text:
I was teaching third grade, and the last unit of the year was the Oregon Trail. Usually I liked to make my lessons goofy and immersive, with characters like Antic Leia and the Howlers, Cheesy de Pizza, and Caesar von Salad, but I wanted this unit to feel serious and real.

So I made an Oregon Trail simulation that was actually dangerous. The students took the names of real people who died on the trail and chose occupations from the 1840s. I made them walk 40 blocks in Manhattan so they could feel some of the hardship of being pioneers. Then we did a chance game that was a mix of the Oregon Trail video game and Dungeons & Dragons dice.

I was in character as Mary, the wagon train captain, and I let the danger keep escalating. Katherine Chubbuck got trapped under a wagon and her legs became infected and she almost died. Dr. Ellis Chapman saved her when Katie rolled a 3. The whole class went wild celebrating, and Katie kept saying that she almost died.

At some point I realized that the students loved the danger more than I did, so after that I replaced the peril with adopting a baby wolf named Yenny the Benny. We got to Oregon pretty quickly after that, homesteaded, made cornbread, and danced to “September.”

Years later, when Katie was in ninth grade, the first thing she said to me was, “Do you remember when I almost died on the Oregon Trail?” and I said yes.

recall_text:
I was teaching third grade, and the last unit of the year was the Oregon Trail. Usually I did goofy, immersive games with silly names and letters, but with the Oregon Trail I wanted it to feel serious and real, even though the kids were nine.

I made an Oregon Trail simulation. The students took the names of real people who had died. They chose occupations from the 1840s. We did a 40-block walk through Manhattan so they could feel how long and hard the journey was. Then we played a chance game that was sort of a mix of the Oregon Trail computer game and Dungeons & Dragons dice.

I was Mary, the wagon train captain, and I wore a bonnet. I hinted that someone could die, and the kids became completely obsessed with the danger. There was also a snake oil salesman episode that made them throw up for a day, and they loved it.

At one point Katie, or Katherine Chubbuck, was almost killed under a wagon. Her legs were infected, and it was very dramatic. Ellis, or Dr. Chapman, saved her on a roll of three. After that I backed away from the danger and made things gentler. I gave them a baby wolf named Yenny the Benny, and then they got to Oregon quickly. We celebrated with cornbread and a dance party. Years later, Katie still remembered almost dying.

I made an Oregon Trail simulation where the students became pioneers. I gave them the names of real dead travelers, using first names and surnames like Chapman and Blunderfield, and they chose authentic 1840s jobs. To help them feel how hard the trail was, I took the whole class on a forty-block walk through Manhattan.

The game was a mix of the Oregon Trail computer game and Dungeons & Dragons dice. Each day there were events, choices, and rolls. I was wearing a bonnet and playing Mary, the captain of the wagon train. A boy named Alex Bacon kept asking if someone could die.

At one point Katie, or Katherine, Chubbuck was almost killed in a wagon accident. Her legs were infected, and Dr. Ellis Chapman saved her on a roll of three. After that I think I took the danger out of it. We adopted a baby wolf named Yenny the Benny, got to Oregon quickly, and celebrated by making cornbread and dancing to “September.”

Years later, the thing Katie said first was, “Do you remember when I almost died on the Oregon Trail?”

recall_text:
A teacher was narrating about teaching third grade, and the last unit was the Oregon Trail. Usually she did goofy immersive games with characters like Cheesy de Pizza and Caesar von Salad, and a stuffed animal band called Antic Leia and the Howlers, but she wanted the Oregon Trail to feel serious and real.

She told the class it was going to be a dangerous game. The students became pioneers and got names from real people who died on the trail, so Alex became Alex Bacon. They chose authentic 1840s jobs. She took them on a 40-block walk in Manhattan so they could feel what the trail was like, and told them that kids walked and the wagons held sick people, supplies, and maybe even a piano.

She made a chance-based simulation that mixed the Oregon Trail video game with Dungeons & Dragons dice. There were daily events, choices, and rolls. One example was crossing a river, deciding between a ferryman and fording the wagons. She played Mary, the wagon train captain, wearing a homemade bonnet.

The class kept asking whether someone would die. In the Rockies, Katherine Chubbuck got trapped under a wagon and her legs became infected. She asked, “did I die?” Dr. Ellis Chapman could save her unless a six was rolled. Katie rolled a three and survived, and the class erupted.

After that the teacher took away the danger. They adopted a baby wolf named Yenny the Benny, got to Oregon quickly, made cornbread, and danced to “September.” Years later, when Katie was in ninth grade, she said, “Do you remember when I almost died on the Oregon Trail?” and the teacher said yes.

recall_text:
The narrator taught third grade by creating immersive, goofy worlds and games. The last unit was the Oregon Trail, and it was treated very seriously, meant to feel real even though westward expansion was complicated.

The students became pioneers and were given real dead-traveler surnames. Alex became Alex Bacon. They chose jobs from the 1840s, took a 40-block walk in Manhattan to feel what the trail was like, and the class used a chance game that mixed the Oregon Trail video game with D&D dice.

The teacher, dressed as Mary in a bonnet, warned that someone might die, and the class loved that sense of danger. There was also a snake oil salesman trick that made them “throw up” and lose a day, which made them even more excited and kept them asking whether anyone was going to die.

In the Rockies, Katherine Chubbuck, called Katie, got trapped under a wagon. An infection got worse and she almost died. Dr. Ellis Chapman stepped in, and only a roll of 6 meant death. Katie rolled a 3 and survived, and the class celebrated wildly.

recall_text:
The teacher narrates teaching third grade, and the last unit is the Oregon Trail. Usually the teacher does goofy immersive games as a kind of puppet master, with things like a stuffed animal rock band called Antic Leia and the Howlers and other silly names, but wanted the Oregon Trail to feel serious and real.

So the teacher created a pioneer simulation. The students took the names of real people who died on the Oregon Trail, so Alex became Alex Bacon. They chose 1840s occupations. They also took a 40-block Manhattan walk to feel what the journey was like, with wagon and water-fountain jokes along the way.

The teacher combined the Oregon Trail video game with Dungeons & Dragons dice, with daily events, choices, and rolls. The teacher was Mary, the wagon train captain, wearing a bonnet, and hinted that someone could die. The class got excited by the danger.

At one point Katie, or Katherine Chubbuck, was trapped under a wagon. Her legs got infected and she nearly died. Dr. Ellis Chapman saved her when Katie rolled a 3 instead of a 6. After that, the teacher took away the danger and gave them a baby wolf named Yenny the Benny. They got to Oregon quickly, made cornbread, and danced to “September.”

Years later, when Katie was in ninth grade, she said, “Do you remember when I almost died on the Oregon Trail?” and the teacher said yes.

recall_text:
I was teaching third grade, and the last unit of the year was the Oregon Trail. Usually I liked goofy immersive games with silly names and fake letters, but this time I wanted it to feel serious and real, even though the kids were nine.

I made an Oregon Trail simulation. The students took the names of real people who had died, chose occupations from the 1840s, and took a forty-block walk through Manhattan so they could feel how much the pioneers had to walk. The class traveled by making choices and rolling dice, kind of like the Oregon Trail video game mixed with Dungeons & Dragons.

At one point Alex Bacon asked if it was a game and if they could die. I said it was a dangerous game and maybe someone might die. After that the kids got obsessed with the danger and kept asking if someone was going to die.

There was a snake oil salesman, and because of him they lost a day throwing up. Later Katherine Chubbuck got trapped under a wagon and her legs got infected and she almost died, but Dr. Ellis Chapman saved her on a roll of three. After that I took the danger out of it. They adopted a baby wolf named Yenny the Benny, got to Oregon quickly, and made cornbread and danced to “September.” Years later Katie still remembered almost dying on the Oregon Trail.

recall_text:
I’m a teacher talking about teaching third grade, and the last unit is the Oregon Trail. Usually I do goofy, immersive games with silly characters and letters, but I wanted this unit to feel serious and real even though the kids were only nine.

I made an Oregon Trail simulation. The students took the names of real people who had died, chose occupations from the 1840s, took a 40-block walk through Manhattan so they could feel what the journey was like, and played a chance-based game that mixed the Oregon Trail video game with Dungeons & Dragons dice.

One student, Alex Bacon, kept asking if someone could die. I was dressed as Mary in a bonnet, and I said yes, even though I didn’t really intend for that to happen. But the class got excited by the danger. There was even a snake-oil episode where they “throw up,” and they loved it.

In the Rockies, Katherine Chubbuck got trapped and infected and almost died, but Dr. Ellis Chapman saved her on a roll of three. After that I took the danger out of the game. They adopted a baby wolf named Yenny the Benny, got to Oregon quickly, made cornbread, and danced to “September.” A year later, when she was in ninth grade, Katie said, “Do you remember when I almost died on the Oregon Trail?”

recall_text:
I taught third grade by creating immersive, goofy worlds where I was basically the puppet master. The last unit I did was the Oregon Trail, and even though westward expansion was complicated, I treated it very seriously and wanted it to feel real.

The class became pioneers. I used the surnames of real travelers who had died, and the students had jobs from the 1840s. We took a 40-block walk through Manhattan so they could feel some of the hardship of the trail. Along the way I had to improvise when people complained about the wagon or about water.

I also designed an Oregon Trail game that was based on chance, kind of mixing the video game with Dungeons & Dragons. There were daily events, choices, and dice rolls that determined what happened. I was Mary, wearing a homemade bonnet, and I was the captain of the wagon train.

The students became completely obsessed with whether someone was going to die. Katie, or Katherine, Chubbuck got trapped under a wagon, and her infection kept getting worse and she almost died. Then Dr. Ellis Chapman saved her on a roll of 3, and everyone celebrated like crazy.

recall_text:
I teach third grade, and the last unit of the year is the Oregon Trail. Usually I do goofy immersive games as a kind of puppet master, with things like Antic Leia and the Howlers, cheesy de pizza, and caesar von salad, but I wanted this one to feel serious and real, though not with the full moral complexity.

I created an Oregon Trail simulation where the students became pioneers using the names of real dead travelers and their 1840s jobs. Alex became Alex Bacon. I took the class on a 40-block walk in Manhattan so they could feel the journey. I told them kids didn’t ride in wagons except if they were sick or supplies or a piano. At a water fountain I improvised something like, “a stream! let us partake.”

The game mixed the Oregon Trail video game with Dungeons & Dragons dice. I was in a bonnet as Mary, the wagon train captain. The students loved the danger and kept asking if someone was going to die. A snake oil salesman conned them, and they “throw up” and lose a day, which they loved.

In the Rockies there was a crisis when the wagon overturned and Katherine Chubbuck, Katie, was trapped. Her legs were infected and she nearly died. Dr. Ellis Chapman saved her. She would only die on a 6, and Katie rolled a 3. After that I avoided danger. There was a baby wolf named Yenny the Benny, then a speedy safe trip to Oregon, and cornbread and a dance party to “September.” Years later Katie first said, “Do you remember when I almost died on the Oregon Trail?” and I said yes.

recall_text:
The story is narrated by a teacher teaching third grade, and the last unit is the Oregon Trail. She usually does goofy, immersive games with silly characters and letters, but she wants this unit to feel serious and real even though the kids are nine.

She creates an Oregon Trail simulation for the class. The students take the names of real people who died, choose 1840s occupations, and walk 40 blocks in Manhattan so they can feel the journey. The game works through choices plus dice, kind of like the Oregon Trail video game mixed with Dungeons & Dragons.

One student, Alex Bacon, keeps asking if someone could die. The teacher is wearing a bonnet and acting as Mary, the wagon train captain, and she says yes even though she does not intend for anyone to die. The class gets excited by the danger. There is also a snake oil salesman episode that makes them “throw up,” and they love it.

In the Rockies, Katherine Chubbuck gets trapped and infected and almost dies, but Dr. Ellis Chapman saves her on a roll of three, when only a six would have meant death. After that, the teacher takes the danger out of the game. A baby wolf named Yenny the Benny joins them, they get to Oregon quickly, and they make cornbread and dance to “September.”

Years later, Katie’s first comment is, “Do you remember when I almost died on the Oregon Trail?”

recall_text:
I was teaching third grade, and the last unit was the Oregon Trail. Usually I did goofy immersive games with characters like Antic Leia and the Howlers, Cheesy de Pizza, and Caesar von Salad, but I wanted the Oregon Trail to feel serious and real.

I created a dangerous Oregon Trail simulation. The students took the names of real people who had died, chose 1840s occupations, took a 40-block walk in Manhattan to feel what the journey was like, and then used a chance game that mixed the Oregon Trail video game with Dungeons & Dragons dice.

I was Mary, the wagon train captain, wearing a bonnet, and I let the danger escalate. Katie, or Katherine Chubbuck, got trapped under a wagon. Her infection got worse and worse, and she kept asking, “did I die?” Ellis, or Dr. Chapman, saved her. You only died on a six, and Katie rolled a three, so she survived, and the class erupted.

I realized the students loved danger more than I did, so I replaced the wild-animal peril with adopting a baby wolf named Yenny the Benny. We reached Oregon quickly, homesteaded, made cornbread, and danced to “September.” A year later Katie still remembered “when I almost died on the Oregon Trail.”

recall_text:
The narrator is a teacher teaching third grade, and the last unit is the Oregon Trail. Usually she does goofy, immersive games with silly characters or bands, but she wants this unit to feel serious and real, even though the kids are 9 and the westward expansion is complicated.

She creates an Oregon Trail simulation. The students take the names of real people who died. They choose 1840s occupations. They do a 40-block walk in Manhattan to feel what the journey was like. They also play a chance-based game that mixes the Oregon Trail video game with Dungeons & Dragons dice.

One student, Alex Bacon, keeps asking if someone could die. The teacher is wearing a bonnet and acting as Mary, the wagon train captain, and she says yes even though she does not intend for anyone to die. The class gets excited by the danger. There is also a snake oil salesman episode that makes them throw up, and they love it.

Later, in the Rockies, Katherine Chubbuck gets trapped and infected and almost dies. Dr. Ellis Chapman saves her on a roll of 3, even though only a 6 meant death. The class celebrates wildly. After that, the teacher takes away the danger and gives them a baby wolf named Yenny the Benny. They get to Oregon quickly, make cornbread, and dance to “September.”

A year later, when Katie is in ninth grade, the first thing she says is, “Do you remember when I almost died on the Oregon Trail?”

I was teaching third grade, and the last unit of the year was the Oregon Trail. Usually I did goofy, immersive games where I was like a puppet master, with things like Antic Leia and the Howlers and cheesy de pizza, but I wanted this one to feel serious and real even though the kids were nine.

I made an Oregon Trail simulation where the students became pioneers and got the names of real people who had died on the trail. Alex became Alex Bacon. They chose jobs from the 1840s. I took the class on a 40-block walk through Manhattan and explained that the kids walked and the wagons were for sick people and supplies and even a piano. At one point I used a water fountain as a stream.

I designed it as a chance-based game that mixed the Oregon Trail video game with Dungeons & Dragons dice. I wore a bonnet and was Mary, the wagon train captain. The students loved the danger and kept asking if someone might die. A snake oil salesman conned them, and they all threw up and lost a day, which they loved.

In the Rockies, Katherine Chubbuck, Katie, got trapped under a wagon. Her infection got worse and she asked, “Did I die?” I panicked until Dr. Ellis Chapman remembered that she was a doctor. Death only happened on a six, and Katie rolled a three, so she survived, and the whole class celebrated wildly.

After that I backed off the danger. A baby wolf named Yenny the Benny joined us, and we got to Oregon quickly. We made cornbread and danced to “September.” Years later, when Katie was in ninth grade, she said, “Do you remember when I almost died on the Oregon Trail?” and I said yes.

recall_text:
A teacher was telling about teaching third grade, and the last unit was the Oregon Trail. Usually she did goofy, immersive games with silly characters or bands, but she wanted this unit to feel serious and real, even though westward expansion was complicated for nine-year-olds.

She made an Oregon Trail simulation. The students took the names of real people who died on the trail and chose 1840s occupations. They did a 40-block walk in Manhattan to feel what the journey was like. Then they played a chance-based game that was a mix of the Oregon Trail video game and Dungeons & Dragons dice.

She was in character as Mary, the wagon train captain, and said that someone might die. The students got obsessed with the danger. They loved the setbacks, like buying snake-oil elixir and then “throwing up” for a day.

There was a dark scene where Katherine Chubbuck, Katie, got trapped under a wagon. An infection got worse and she almost died, but Dr. Ellis Chapman saved her on a roll of three. After that, the teacher backed away from the danger and gave them a baby wolf named Yenny the Benny. They got to Oregon quickly after that and celebrated with cornbread and a dance party to “September.”

Years later, Katie still remembered it and said, “Do you remember when I almost died on the Oregon Trail?”

The teacher’s last third-grade unit was the Oregon Trail. Usually she did goofy immersive games as a puppet-master teacher, but she wanted this one to feel serious and real because of the complexity of westward expansion.

The class became pioneers. They used the names of real dead travelers and had 1840s jobs. They took a 40-block walk through Manhattan so the students could feel some of the hardship of the trail. The teacher improvised when people complained about the wagon or about water.

She mixed the Oregon Trail video game with Dungeons & Dragons dice. There were daily events, choices, and rolls. She wore a bonnet and became Mary, the wagon train captain. The students were especially focused on whether somebody might die.

Katie, or Katherine Chubbuck, almost died after a wagon accident and infected legs. Dr. Ellis Chapman saved her on a roll of three. After that, the teacher moved away from the danger part and had them adopt a baby wolf named Yenny the Benny. They reached Oregon quickly after that and celebrated with cornbread and a dance to “September.” Years later, Katie still remembered almost dying.

The class even took a 40-block Manhattan walk so they could feel what the journey was like. The teacher told them that children walked, and that wagons were for sick people, supplies, and maybe even a piano.

The class kept asking if someone was going to die. In the Rockies, a wagon overturned and Katherine Chubbuck, Katie, was trapped, and her legs got infected. The teacher panicked, but Dr. Ellis Chapman remembered that she was a doctor. Katie would survive unless she rolled a six, and she rolled a three, so the class celebrated wildly.

After that near-death moment, the teacher took away the danger. Wild animals turned into a baby wolf named Yenny the Benny, and they adopted it for the rest of the trip. They got to Oregon quickly, homesteaded, did a budget, made cornbread, and danced to “September.” Years later, when Katie was in ninth grade, the first thing she said was, “Do you remember when I almost died on the Oregon Trail?”

recall_text:
I’m a teacher, and every year I narrate my teaching to my third grade class. The last unit is the Oregon Trail. Usually I do goofy immersive games with silly characters and letters, but I wanted this unit to feel serious and real, even though the kids were nine.

So I created an Oregon Trail simulation. The students took the names of real people who died. They chose 1840s occupations. We took a forty-block walk in Manhattan so they could feel what the journey was like, and we played a chance game that mixed the Oregon Trail video game with Dungeons & Dragons dice.

I dressed as Mary, the wagon train captain, and wore a bonnet. I told the class that someone might die. The kids became obsessed with the danger. There was a snake oil salesman episode that made them throw up for a day, and they loved it.

At one point, on a Rockies scene, Katherine Chubbuck, Katie, was trapped under a wagon. Her legs were infected and she nearly died. Dr. Ellis Chapman saved her when Katie rolled a 3 instead of a 6, and the class celebrated wildly.

turn_logs.content: So it's the last unit of the year I'm teaching third grade. And the last unit is the oregon trail. And I am prepared to have my students really live the oregon trail. This is how I taught third grade: I would create a world and then run it like a puppet master um. I uh and and, a lot of those times, those worlds were goofy. Like we have always a game uh we got letters from a stuffed animal rock band named Antic Leia, and the Howlers who were lost across the united states and we were studying geography so to help them. We had to study the states. Uh we got letters from time machines. My characters had names like cheesy de pizza and caesar von salad. Um. i was not a serious teacher. uh but now this is the oregon trail. This is a serious time and this is also a really complicated time in American history. Um but to be totally honest, I'm not sure I can get at the like historical and moral complexities of westward expansion with nine year olds. They have trouble taking the perspective of their little sister. So I'm not really sure I can do that, but I know I can get at the gravity of it right? This is pioneers. Two thousand miles across the united states which weren't the united states yet across the Rockies, leaving everything they know risking everything they have. Blizzards and hunger and all these things and, so at least I can get it's really real and at least I can get my kids to feel like it's really real. So I come to my class and I say we're gonna be doing the oregon trail and this one smart aleck kid named Alex says, "well will it be a game?" cuz he knows it's always a game. And I say, "yeah, but it's gonna be a dangerous game." And they're pretty psyched about that. So what I've planned is like a simulation: we're gonna take on characters of pioneers and we're going to travel the oregon trail on a wagon train. So first we have to choose names for our characters. I downloaded and printed the names of real people who died on the oregon trail. It's pretty authentic. And so they can have their first names but they have to have last names like Chapman and Blunderfield and Alex is now Alex Bacon. And then they have to choose occupations, and all the girls wanna be pop stars. And I tell them, "there were no pop stars on the oregon trail. Choose authentic occupations from the eighteen forties." so okay, so great. There are farmers and there are gold miners and there's a couple of doctors and we're we're good. But before we start i want them to feel what it really felt like to walk for that long. So i was here in Manhattan. I took them on a forty block walk.  It's about two miles. It's not that long. It's long if you're a nine year old, I guess. And it's a beautiful day you know we're going up the west side we're going up the Hudson. and uh Alex Bacon says to me, "well I wouldn't have had to walk. I would have ridden in the wagon." And i said, "Aha. No no. Children never rode in the wagons. The wagons were for if there was someone sick, or our supplies or if we had a piano." Cuz i have done my research. And then another kid says, "well I'm thirsty and I say well there were no water fountains on the oregon trail." And he says, "well there's a water fountain right there." And I think about the parent phone call. I do not wanna get about withholding water from a child. And I think fast and I say, "Ah! a stream! How fortunate. Let us partake." And so we finally get back and we're hot and sweaty, but we're ready. We're ready to go on our journey. And the way I designed it is... Previously, all of my games were just fiction. Like I would just write a letter and then they would respond and I would write another letter that night. I always knew what was gonna happen. But now i wanna play a little more dangerously, because it was all luck what happened on the oregon trail right? So I have designed a game of chance. um. I have combined. Do you guys know the oregon trail video game? fans okay. uh. I've designed. uh I've I've. combined the oregon trail video game with principles of dungeons and dragons,  the role playing game with dice. So what we're gonna do is, every day I'm gonna tell them what happened on the trail that day. They're gonna make some choices about what they wanna do. And then we're gonna roll dice to see if they succeeded or failed. So I'll give you an example. We get to a river and they have to decide. Do they wanna pay a ferryman or do they want to ford their wagons, and they decide to ford their wagons, we roll to find out if their wagons sink or floated. That kind of thing. So it's easy. great. alright. So the first day starts, and I have this bonnet that I've sewn out of old upholstery material, and I put on this bonnet, and i tell them, "I am Mary, your wagon train captain. We are all here for different reasons but we will have to work together to get through the bad weather and the hunger and the wild animals that await us." And Alex Bacon says, "Excuse me Mary, this is a dangerous game. Could we die? And I was a little in character at that point. And I will also admit I wanted to take Alex down a peg. So i said, "Sure, people died on the oregon trail all the time. Someone might die." And this shiver of excitement goes across my class. They liked my stuffed animal rock band but they are into danger and I know i'm not gonna let anyone die. Like I'm not gonna let it get there right? No one's gonna die on the oregon trail, but the idea that someone might gets them wanting to come to social studies every day, so this is okay. So we're off. We're tracking our mileage we're rolling dice or making tough choices and at some point. uh i have them meet a snake oil salesman. who offers to sell them an elixir that will make them stronger and faster and get to oregon city quicker. And something you need to know about nine year olds, a lot of them, pretty much all of them, don't know what snake oil salesmen are. I say this to you and you know this is shorthand for like a con man right? But to them it's just someone else they don't know about, like taxes, like that it's just a thing like a grown up thing. Okay snake oil salesman. So they decide to buy the elixir cause they wanna go get there faster. So we roll to see how much stronger and faster they got, and of course we all know the answer is none faster uh. It's snake oil so i tell them um. actually that was a con. You are throwing up for a day. You lose a day of travel, and I think they're gonna be really annoyed that they got slowed down but they are psyched. They got to throw up in social studies. They're talking about it for days. My game is a hit. The problem is, every day before we start, someone says to me, "is someone gonna die today?" "Is someone gonna die today?". And I've been putting them off and putting them off, but my game is going so well and we're getting towards the Rockies. And I figure, you know what, I'm gonna give them just a brush with death. So I write, I write out a bunch of possibilities for that day. And um the next time someone asks me is someone gonna die today, I say, "we have been lucky thus far, but the rockies lie ahead, the most treacherous part of our journey. Who knows what might happen." So I put on the bonnet, and that's what I did. I loved that action. And i set the scene for the morning, "In the early morning light, on a Rocky mountain pass, a wagon hits a rock and is overturned. Someone is trapped beneath the wagon. Let us roll to find out who it is." I'm not proud of this. I take off the bonnet and we have like a system of rules to figure out. Different kids have different numbers and I roll, and it's this little girl Katie I know. Her oregon trail name is Katherine Chubbuck. She's a farmer. She's one of these kids who always has really messy hair and sounds like she's been smoking since she was three. And she has to come to the front of the class and I say, "Katherine Chubbuck, your legs have been trapped beneath the wagon. Roll to find out if you get free and what happens." And she rolls, and she gets free. But her legs have been infected. I wrote these possibilities and this is the first time I'm thinking, "why did i write that possibility?" This is getting really dark, and I say, "Katherine Chubbuck, roll to find out if your infection gets better or worse." And she rolls, and it gets worse, and she looks at me and just goes, "did i die?" And as soon as she says it, I realize how much trouble I am in. I haven't written any more possibilities. I didn't think we would get this far. So what happens next? Do we have a funeral on the side of the oregon trail for Katherine Chubbuck? Is that the parent phone call that I get for having traumatized a girl for killing her on the oregon trail? "Bad teachers kill kids on the oregon trail." And I am not a bad teacher, or so i thought. This is all the stuff that's happening in my head. I'm thinking so much about it. A lot of it is very existential and then all of a sudden, from the back of the class, this little girl Ellis whose oregon trail name is Dr Ellis Chapman just goes, "Wait, I'm a doctor!" And I'm like, "thank the lord". Dr Chapman brings her doctor bag. She knows how to heal the wound. Ellis Chapman comes up to the front of the room. I say, "the only way you roll to find out what happens, the only way you die is if you roll a six. That's the only way you die." The class is holding their breath. As Katie rolls, she does the lucky like shake thing and then someone just goes, "shake them again!" She shakes, and she rolls, and it's a three and she survives. I know, I know, in my class it's like the end of Apollo thirteen. Kids are throwing papers in the air and like hugging each other, and Ellis is hugging Katie, and Katie's just going, "I almost died. I almost died." And I am so glad we agreed to bring a doctor on the oregon trail with us. She couldn't hunt but she was very useful. And the problem is... So that was great. The problem is, we still have seven hundred and twenty miles to oregon city, and I'm exhausted. I can't remember a time before we were walking the oregon trail. And the next day, you know I had all the stuff planned, and the next day I get to class, I put my bonnet on, I tell them, "we hear animal noises in the bushes." And Alex Bacon is right on it. He goes, "Is it wild animals? Are we in danger?" And he says it, and I realize they love the danger. I'm the one who doesn't want the danger. And I throw my plan out the window. It was wild animals and we were in danger actually but I forget about that. I say, "No, it is a baby animal with a broken leg, who we must adopt for the rest of the trip." And they all do the third-grade baby animal noise which is aw. And I say, "let us roll to find out what species of baby animal we will be adopting. Is it a baby bunny a baby fox or a baby wolf?" It's a baby wolf. They name him Yenny the Benny. They love him very much, and he follows us all the way to oregon. And we get to oregon in record time. I mean, forget pioneers walking. This is amazon prime, two day shipping, to get to oregon city. Nothing bad happens between the Rockies and oregon city and when we get there, we do, we homestead and we do our budget. So we do all that stuff but we also make cornbread, and we have a dance party to "September" by Earth, Wind and Fire, which is not historically accurate. But that is the kind of oregon trail I wanna be on at that point. So that's the oregon trail but I have to tell you guys, about a year ago I ran into Katie on the street on broadway, and she's in ninth grade now. She looks exactly the same except that she's been stretched, you know. And I recognized her right away and she recognized me, and we hugged and I said how are you and she said and the first thing she said to me was, "do you remember when I almost died on the oregon trail?" and i said, "yeah Katie, I absolutely remember."

Joe Matson, a baseball pitcher, was at home during a snowstorm with his sister Clara and his mother, Mrs. Matson, called “Momsey.” He was talking with them when he got a letter from Mr. Gregory of Pittston. The letter said that the St. Louis Nationals, or Cardinals, might draft him from the Central League to the major leagues. It meant more money and fame, but also hard work.

There was also another letter from Mabel Varley. She wrote that she and her brother Reggie were coming through town that day and would stop briefly, and Joe planned to meet them at the station.

Joe went to the depot. The station master said the trains were late. Later he told Joe that the express carrying Mabel and Reggie was snowed in at Deep Rock Cut, five miles away. Joe became worried about how to help.
