"Out at first! Say, Momsey, I hope I didn't hit you!"

"No, you didn't," and she laughed now. "But what does it all mean? Are you practicing so early in the season? Oh, my carpet! It will be ruined!" she went on, as she saw the water. "But I'm glad I didn't bring in a good jug. Did you hurt your hand?"

"Nary a hurt," said Joe, with a smile. "Ha! I'll save you from a wetting!" he exclaimed, as he stooped quickly and picked up an unopened letter, the address of which was in a girlish hand.

"Get the mop, while you're at it," advised Clara. A little later Joe had sopped up the water, and quiet was restored.

"And now suppose you tell us all about it," suggested Mrs. Mason. "Why were you practicing gymnastics, Joe?" and she smiled at her athletic son.

"I was just telling Clara that my pitching arm was likely to bring me in more money this year, Momsey, and I was giving it a twirl, when you happened to get in my way. Now I'll tell you all about it. It's this letter," and Joe held out the one he had been reading.

"Are you sure it isn't the other?" asked Clara, with a sly look at her brother, for she had glanced at the writing on the unopened envelope Joe had picked up from the floor. "Let me read that other letter, Joe," she teased.

"A little later -- maybe!" he parried. "But this one," and he fluttered the open sheet in his hand, "this one is from Mr. Gregory, manager of the Pittston team, with whom I have the honor to be associated," and Joe bowed low to his mother and sister. "Mr. Gregory gives me a bit of news. It is nothing less than that the manager of the St. Louis Nationals is negotiating for the services of yours truly -- your humble servant, Joseph Matson," and again the young ball player bowed, and laughed.

"Joe, you don't mean it!" cried his sister. "You're going to belong to a major league team!" for Clara was almost as ardent a baseball "fan" as was her brother.

"Well, it looks like it, Sis," replied Joe, slowly, as he glanced at the letter again. "Of course it isn't settled, but Mr. Gregory says I'm pretty sure to be drafted to St. Louis."

"Drafted!" exclaimed his mother. "That sounds like war times, when they used to draft men to go to the front. Do you mean you haven't any choice in the matter, Joe?"

"Well, that's about it, Momsey," the young man explained. "You see, baseball is pretty well organized. It has to be, to make it the success it is," he added frankly, "though lots of people are opposed to the system. But I haven't been in it long enough to find fault, even if I wanted to -- which I don't."

"But it seems queer that you can't stay with the Pittston team if you want to," said Mrs. Matson.

"I don't know as I want to," spoke Joe, slowly, "especially when I'll surely get more money with St. Louis, besides having the honor of pitching for a major league team, even if it isn't one of the top-notchers, and a pennant winner. "You see," he resumed, "when I signed a contract with the Pittstons, of the Central League, I gave them the right to control my services as long as I played baseball. I'll get more money and fame.

"That is, I hope I will," and Joe spoke more soberly. "I know I'm not going to have any snap of it. It's going to be hard work from the word go, for there will be other pitchers on the St. Louis team, and I'll have to do my best to make a showing against them.

recall_text:
Joe Matson was a pitcher on the Pittston team in the Central League. He lived at home with his mother, Mrs. Matson, called “Momsey,” and his sister Clara. One snowy morning the mail came and Joe got an important letter from Mr. Gregory. The letter said that the St. Louis Nationals, or Cardinals, were negotiating to draft Joe from Pittston to the major leagues. It was not final yet, but it seemed likely.

Joe was excited and began thinking about the chance to go up higher, with more money and fame, though he also knew there would be hard competition and hoped he would “make good.” In his excitement he swung his pitching arm and knocked a jug of water from his mother’s hands and broke it. Then he had to clean up the mess while Clara teased him because there was another unopened letter.

That second letter was from Mabel Varley. Mabel and her brother Reggie were friends of Joe and were coming by train that day and stopping at a hotel. Joe went to the station in the worsening snow to meet them. Later the station master told him that their express had been stalled or snowed in at Deep Rock Cut, about five miles away, and might be held there for days. Joe was alarmed because his friends were on that train.

recall_text:
Joe Matson was a young pitcher in the Central League at Pittston. He lived with his mother, Mrs. Matson, whom they called “Momsey,” and his sister Clara. Joe knew Mabel Varley and her brother Reggie, and cared a good deal about them.

One morning at breakfast, or when the mail came, there was a snowstorm going on. Joe got a letter from Mr. Gregory. The letter said that St. Louis, the Nationals or Cardinals, might draft Joe from Pittston into the major leagues. It was not settled for certain, but it seemed likely. The change would mean more money and more fame for Joe, though there would also be harder competition.

Joe was very excited over this news. He swung his pitching arm around and in his excitement knocked over and broke Mrs. Matson’s water jug. He joked about it afterward. He explained to Clara and to his mother how the baseball draft worked.

There was also a second letter, from Mabel Varley. She wrote that she and Reggie were coming through town that day and might stop off. Joe went to the depot in the snow, which was getting worse. Later he learned that their express train had been snowed in at Deep Rock Cut, about five miles away. It had not been wrecked, but was blocked there by the storm.

"Out at first! Say, Momsey, I hope I didn't hit you!"

"No, you didn't," and she laughed now. "But what does it all mean? Are you practicing so early in the season? Oh, my carpet! It will be ruined!" she went on, as she saw the water. "But I'm glad I didn't bring in a good jug. Did you hurt your hand?"

"Nary a hurt," said Joe, with a smile. "Ha! I'll save you from a wetting!" he exclaimed, as he stooped quickly and picked up an unopened letter, the address of which was in a girlish hand.

"Get the mop, while you're at it," advised Clara. A little later Joe had sopped up the water, and quiet was restored.

"And now suppose you tell us all about it," suggested Mrs. Mason. "Why were you practicing gymnastics, Joe?" and she smiled at her athletic son.

"I was just telling Clara that my pitching arm was likely to bring me in more money this year, Momsey, and I was giving it a twirl, when you happened to get in my way. Now I'll tell you all about it. It's this letter," and Joe held out the one he had been reading.

"Joe, you don't mean it!" cried his sister. "You're going to belong to a major league team!" for Clara was almost as ardent a baseball "fan" as was her brother.

"You see," he resumed, "when I signed a contract with the Pittstons, of the Central League, I gave them the right to control my services as long as I played baseball. "Well, there's nothing definite. The managers are laying their plans for the Spring work, and he says I'm being considered. He adds he will be sorry to lose me."

"Oh, I wouldn't go as far as to say that!" cried Joe, "though I appreciate your feeling, Sis. I had a good bit of luck, winning some of the games the way I did. Joe got a letter from Mr. Gregory, the Pittston manager, saying that the St. Louis Nationals, or Cardinals, might draft him into the major leagues. It meant more money for Joe, but he would have to compete hard, and he hoped he could “make good.”

recall_text:
Joe Matson, a baseball pitcher, was at home during a snowstorm with his sister Clara and his mother, Mrs. Matson, whom they called “Momsey.” They were talking at home when Joe got a letter from Mr. Gregory of Pittston. The letter said that the St. Louis Nationals might draft him from the Central League into the major leagues. It meant more money and honor, but it was not definite yet.

There was also another letter from Mabel Varley. She and her brother Reggie were traveling and were stopping in town that day, and would likely come to see the Matsons. Joe planned to meet them.

Later Joe went to the depot as the storm got worse. Afterward the station master said that the express carrying Mabel and Reggie had been snowed in at Deep Rock Cut, about five miles away. Joe began to wonder how he could help.

"Whew!" whistled Joe Matson, the astonishment on his bronzed face being indicated by his surprised exclamation of:

"Well, what do you know about that, Sis?"

"What is it, Joe?" asked his sister Clara, as she looked up from a letter she was reading to see her brother staring at a sheet of paper he had just withdrawn from an envelope, for the morning mail had been delivered a few minutes before. "What is it?" the girl went on, laying aside her own correspondence. "Is it anything serious -- anything about father's business? Don't tell me there is more trouble, Joe!"

"I'm not going to, Clara. It isn't trouble, but, if what he says is true, it's going to make a big difference to me," and Joe looked out of the window, across a snowy expanse of yard, and gazed at, without consciously seeing, a myriad of white flakes swirling down through the wintry air.

"No, it isn't exactly trouble," went on Joe, "and I suppose I ought to be corkingly glad of it; but I hadn't counted on leaving the Central Baseball League quite so soon."

"Oh, Joe! Have you lost your place?" exclaimed Clara. "And just after you have done so well, too; and helped them win the pennant! I call that a shame! I thought baseball men were better sports than that."

"Listen to her -- my little sister using slang!" laughed Joe.

"Sports isn't slang," defended Clara. "I've heard lots of girls use it. I mean it in the right sense. But have you really lost your place on the team, Joe?"

"Well, not exactly, Sis, but I'm about to, I'm afraid. However, I guess I may as well make the best of it, and be glad. I sure can use the extra money!"

"I certainly don't know what you're talking about," went on Clara, with a helpless look at her big, handsome brother, "and I suppose you'll take your own time in telling me. But I would like to know what it all means, Joe. And about extra money. Who's going to give it to you?"

"Nobody. I'll have to earn it with this pitching arm of mine," and the young baseball player swung it around, as though "winding-up" for a swift delivery.

"Look out, Joe!" cried Clara, but she gave the warning too late.

At that moment Mrs. Matson entered the room with a jug of water, which she intended pouring on a window-box of flowers. Joe's arm struck the jug a glancing blow, and sent it flying, the water spraying over the floor, and the jug itself falling, and cracking into many pieces.

For a moment there was a momentous silence, after two startled screams -- one each from Mrs. Matson and Clara. Then Joe cried gaily:

"Out at first! Say, Momsey, I hope I didn't hit you!"

"No, you didn't," and she laughed now. "But what does it all mean? Are you practicing so early in the season? Oh, my carpet! It will be ruined!" she went on, as she saw the water. "But I'm glad I didn't bring in a good jug. Did you hurt your hand?"

"Nary a hurt," said Joe, with a smile. "Ha! I'll save you from a wetting!" he exclaimed, as he stooped quickly and picked up an unopened letter, the address of which was in a girlish hand.

"Get the mop, while you're at it," advised Clara. A little later Joe had sopped up the water, and quiet was restored.

"And now suppose you tell us all about it," suggested Mrs. Mason. "Why were you practicing gymnastics, Joe?" and she smiled at her athletic son.

"I was just telling Clara that my pitching arm was likely to bring me in more money this year, Momsey, and I was giving it a twirl, when you happened to get in my way. Now I'll tell you all about it. It's this letter," and Joe held out the one he had been reading.

"Are you sure it isn't the other?" asked Clara, with a sly look at her brother, for she had glanced at the writing on the unopened envelope Joe had picked up from the floor. "Let me read that other letter, Joe," she teased.

"A little later -- maybe!" he parried. "But this one," and he fluttered the open sheet in his hand, "this one is from Mr. Gregory, manager of the Pittston team, with whom I have the honor to be associated," and Joe bowed low to his mother and sister. "Mr. Gregory gives me a bit of news. It is nothing less than that the manager of the St. Louis Nationals is negotiating for the services of yours truly -- your humble servant, Joseph Matson," and again the young ball player bowed, and laughed.

"Joe, you don't mean it!" cried his sister. "You're going to belong to a major league team!" for Clara was almost as ardent a baseball "fan" as was her brother.

"Well, it looks like it, Sis," replied Joe, slowly, as he glanced at the letter again. "Of course it isn't settled, but Mr. Gregory says I'm pretty sure to be drafted to St. Louis."

"Drafted!" exclaimed his mother. "That sounds like war times, when they used to draft men to go to the front. Do you mean you haven't any choice in the matter, Joe?"

"Well, that's about it, Momsey," the young man explained. "You see, baseball is pretty well organized. It has to be, to make it the success it is," he added frankly, "though lots of people are opposed to the system. But I haven't been in it long enough to find fault, even if I wanted to -- which I don't."

"But it seems queer that you can't stay with the Pittston team if you want to," said Mrs. Matson.

"I don't know as I want to," spoke Joe, slowly, "especially when I'll surely get more money with St. Louis, besides having the honor of pitching for a major league team, even if it isn't one of the top-notchers, and a pennant winner. So if they want to draft me, let them do their worst!" and he laughed, showing his even, white teeth.

"You see," he resumed, "when I signed a contract with the Pittstons, of the Central League, I gave them the right to control my services as long as I played baseball. I had to agree not to go to any other team without permission, and, in fact, no other organized team would take me unless the Pittston management released me. I went into it with my eyes open.

"And, you see, the Pittston team, being one of the small ones, has to give way to a major league team. That is, any major league team, like the St. Louis Nationals, can call for, or draft, any player in a smaller team. So if they call me I'll have to go. And I'll be glad to. I'll get more money and fame.

"That is, I hope I will," and Joe spoke more soberly. "I know I'm not going to have any snap of it. It's going to be hard work from the word go, for there will be other pitchers on the St. Louis team, and I'll have to do my best to make a showing against them.

"And I will, too!" cried Joe, resolutely. "I'll make good, Momsey!"

"I hope so, my son," she responded, quietly. "You know I was not much in favor of your taking up baseball for a living, but I must say you have done well at it, and after all, if one does one's best at anything, that is what counts. So I hope you make good with the St. Louis team -- I suppose make good is the proper expression," she added, with a smile.

"It'll do first-rate, Momsey," laughed Joe. "Now let's see what else Gregory says."

He glanced over the letter again, and remarked:

"Well, there's nothing definite. The managers are laying their plans for the Spring work, and he says I'm being considered. He adds he will be sorry to lose me."

"I should think he would be!" exclaimed Clara, a flush coming into her cheeks. "You were the best pitcher on his team!"

"Oh, I wouldn't go as far as to say that!" cried Joe, "though I appreciate your feeling, Sis. I had a good bit of luck, winning some of the games the way I did. Well, I guess I'll go look up some St. Louis records, and see what I'm expected to do in the batting average line compared with them," the player went on. "The St. Louis team isn't a wonder, but it's done pretty fair at times, I believe, and it's a step up for me. I'll be more in line for a place on the New York Giants, or the Philadelphia Athletics if I make a good showing in Missouri," finished Joe.

He started from the room, carrying the two letters, one of which he had not yet opened.

"Who's it from?" asked Clara, with a smile, as she pointed to the heavy, square envelope in his hand.

"Oh, one of my many admirers," teased Joe. "I can't tell just which one until I open it. And, just to satisfy your curiosity, I'll do so now," and he proceeded to slit the envelope with his pocket-knife.

"Oh, it's from Mabel Varley!" he exclaimed.

"Just as if you didn't know all the while!" scoffed Clara. "You wouldn't forget her handwriting so soon, Joe Matson."

"Um!" he murmured, non-committally. "Why, this is news!" he cried, suddenly. "Mabel and her brother Reggie are coming here!"

"Here!" exclaimed Clara. "To visit us?"

"Oh, no, not that exactly," Joe went on. "They're on a trip, it seems, and they're going to stop off here for a day or so. Mabel says they'll try to see us. I hope they will."

"I've never met them," observed Clara.

"No," spoke Joe, musingly. "Well, you may soon. Why!" he went on, "they're coming to-day -- on the afternoon express. I must go down to the station to meet them, though the train is likely to be late, if this snow keeps up. Whew! see it come down!" and he went over to the window and looked out.

"It's like a small blizzard," remarked Clara, "and it seems to be growing worse. Doesn't look much like baseball; does it, Joe?"

"I should say not! Say, I believe I'll go down to the station, anyhow, and see what the prospects are. Want to come, Sis?"

"No, thank you. Not in this storm. Where are the Varleys going to stop?"

"At the hotel. Reggie has some business in town, Mabel writes. Well, I sure will be glad to see him again!"

"Him? Her, you mean!" laughed Clara. "Oh, Joe, you are so simple!"

"Humph!" he exclaimed, as he put the two letters into his pocket -- both of great importance to him. "Well, I'll go down to the station."

Joe was soon trudging through the storm on the way to the depot.

"The St. Louis Cardinals!" he mused, as he bent his head to the blast, thinking of the letters in his pocket. "I didn't think I'd be in line for a major league team so soon. I wonder if I can make good?"

Thinking alternately of the pleasure he would have in seeing Miss Mabel Varley, a girl in whom he was more than ordinarily interested, and of the new chance that had come to him, Joe soon reached the depot. His inquiries about the trains were not, however, very satisfactorily answered.

"We can't tell much about them in this storm," the station master said. "All our trains are more or less late. Stop in this afternoon, and I may have some definite information for you."

And later that day, when it was nearly arrival time for the train on which Mabel and Reggie were to come, Joe received some news that startled him.

"There's no use in your waiting, Joe," said the station master, as the young ball player approached him again. "Your train won't be in to-day, and maybe not for several days."

"Why? What's the matter -- a wreck?" cried Joe, a vision of injured friends looming before him.

"Not exactly a wreck, but almost as bad," went on the official. "The train is stalled -- snowed in at Deep Rock Cut, five miles above here, and there's no chance of getting her out."

"Great Scott!" cried Joe. "The express snowed in! Why, I've got friends on that train! I wonder what I can do to help them?"

recall_text:
Joe Matson was a pitcher for Pittston in the Central League. He got a letter from Mr. Gregory saying that St. Louis, the Nationals or Cardinals, might draft him up to the major leagues. It meant more money and fame, but also hard work and having to compete with other pitchers.

At home Joe was talking with his sister Clara and his mother, Mrs. Matson, whom they called Momsey. Joe was swinging his pitching arm around in the house and he hit Mrs. Matson’s water jug and broke it. Then he had to mop up the water. Clara teased him about another letter that he had not opened yet, one in girlish handwriting.

Mabel Varley and her brother Reggie were expected to come by train and stop off in town that day. But the snowstorm kept getting worse. Joe went to the depot and learned that their express was stalled or snowed in at Deep Rock Cut, about five miles away, and that they would not be arriving that day.

"Whew!" whistled Joe Matson, the astonishment on his bronzed face being indicated by his surprised exclamation of:

"Well, what do you know about that, Sis?"

"What is it, Joe?" asked his sister Clara, as she looked up from a letter she was reading to see her brother staring at a sheet of paper he had just withdrawn from an envelope, for the morning mail had been delivered a few minutes before. "What is it?" the girl went on, laying aside her own correspondence. "Is it anything serious -- anything about father's business? Don't tell me there is more trouble, Joe!"

"I'm not going to, Clara. It isn't trouble, but, if what he says is true, it's going to make a big difference to me," and Joe looked out of the window, across a snowy expanse of yard, and gazed at, without consciously seeing, a myriad of white flakes swirling down through the wintry air.

"No, it isn't exactly trouble," went on Joe, "and I suppose I ought to be corkingly glad of it; but I hadn't counted on leaving the Central Baseball League quite so soon."

"Oh, Joe! Have you lost your place?" exclaimed Clara. "And just after you have done so well, too; and helped them win the pennant! I call that a shame! I thought baseball men were better sports than that."

"Listen to her -- my little sister using slang!" laughed Joe.

"Sports isn't slang," defended Clara. "I've heard lots of girls use it. I mean it in the right sense. But have you really lost your place on the team, Joe?"

"Well, not exactly, Sis, but I'm about to, I'm afraid. However, I guess I may as well make the best of it, and be glad. I sure can use the extra money!"

"I certainly don't know what you're talking about," went on Clara, with a helpless look at her big, handsome brother, "and I suppose you'll take your own time in telling me. But I would like to know what it all means, Joe. And about extra money. Who's going to give it to you?"

"Nobody. I'll have to earn it with this pitching arm of mine," and the young baseball player swung it around, as though "winding-up" for a swift delivery.

"Look out, Joe!" cried Clara, but she gave the warning too late.

At that moment Mrs. Matson entered the room with a jug of water, which she intended pouring on a window-box of flowers. Joe's arm struck the jug a glancing blow, and sent it flying, the water spraying over the floor, and the jug itself falling, and cracking into many pieces.

For a moment there was a momentous silence, after two startled screams -- one each from Mrs. Matson and Clara. Then Joe cried gaily:

"Out at first! Say, Momsey, I hope I didn't hit you!"

"No, you didn't," and she laughed now. "But what does it all mean? Are you practicing so early in the season? Oh, my carpet! It will be ruined!" she went on, as she saw the water. "But I'm glad I didn't bring in a good jug. Did you hurt your hand?"

"Nary a hurt," said Joe, with a smile. "Ha! I'll save you from a wetting!" he exclaimed, as he stooped quickly and picked up an unopened letter, the address of which was in a girlish hand.

"Get the mop, while you're at it," advised Clara. A little later Joe had sopped up the water, and quiet was restored.

"And now suppose you tell us all about it," suggested Mrs. Mason. "Why were you practicing gymnastics, Joe?" and she smiled at her athletic son.

"I was just telling Clara that my pitching arm was likely to bring me in more money this year, Momsey, and I was giving it a twirl, when you happened to get in my way. Now I'll tell you all about it. It's this letter," and Joe held out the one he had been reading.

"Are you sure it isn't the other?" asked Clara, with a sly look at her brother, for she had glanced at the writing on the unopened envelope Joe had picked up from the floor. "Let me read that other letter, Joe," she teased.

"A little later -- maybe!" he parried. "But this one," and he fluttered the open sheet in his hand, "this one is from Mr. Gregory, manager of the Pittston team, with whom I have the honor to be associated," and Joe bowed low to his mother and sister. "Mr. Gregory gives me a bit of news. It is nothing less than that the manager of the St. Louis Nationals is negotiating for the services of yours truly -- your humble servant, Joseph Matson," and again the young ball player bowed, and laughed.

"Joe, you don't mean it!" cried his sister. "You're going to belong to a major league team!" for Clara was almost as ardent a baseball "fan" as was her brother.

"Well, it looks like it, Sis," replied Joe, slowly, as he glanced at the letter again. "Of course it isn't settled, but Mr. Gregory says I'm pretty sure to be drafted to St. Louis."

"Drafted!" exclaimed his mother. "That sounds like war times, when they used to draft men to go to the front. Do you mean you haven't any choice in the matter, Joe?"

"Well, that's about it, Momsey," the young man explained. "You see, baseball is pretty well organized. It has to be, to make it the success it is," he added frankly, "though lots of people are opposed to the system. But I haven't been in it long enough to find fault, even if I wanted to -- which I don't."

"But it seems queer that you can't stay with the Pittston team if you want to," said Mrs. Matson.

"I don't know as I want to," spoke Joe, slowly, "especially when I'll surely get more money with St. Louis, besides having the honor of pitching for a major league team, even if it isn't one of the top-notchers, and a pennant winner. So if they want to draft me, let them do their worst!" and he laughed, showing his even, white teeth.

"You see," he resumed, "when I signed a contract with the Pittstons, of the Central League, I gave them the right to control my services as long as I played baseball. I had to agree not to go to any other team without permission, and, in fact, no other organized team would take me unless the Pittston management released me. I went into it with my eyes open.

"And, you see, the Pittston team, being one of the small ones, has to give way to a major league team. That is, any major league team, like the St. Louis Nationals, can call for, or draft, any player in a smaller team. So if they call me I'll have to go. And I'll be glad to. I'll get more money and fame.

"That is, I hope I will," and Joe spoke more soberly. "I know I'm not going to have any snap of it. It's going to be hard work from the word go, for there will be other pitchers on the St. Louis team, and I'll have to do my best to make a showing against them.

"And I will, too!" cried Joe, resolutely. "I'll make good, Momsey!"

"I hope so, my son," she responded, quietly. "You know I was not much in favor of your taking up baseball for a living, but I must say you have done well at it, and after all, if one does one's best at anything, that is what counts. So I hope you make good with the St. Louis team -- I suppose make good is the proper expression," she added, with a smile.

"It'll do first-rate, Momsey," laughed Joe. "Now let's see what else Gregory says."

He glanced over the letter again, and remarked:

"Well, there's nothing definite. The managers are laying their plans for the Spring work, and he says I'm being considered. He adds he will be sorry to lose me."

"I should think he would be!" exclaimed Clara, a flush coming into her cheeks. "You were the best pitcher on his team!"

"Oh, I wouldn't go as far as to say that!" cried Joe, "though I appreciate your feeling, Sis. I had a good bit of luck, winning some of the games the way I did. Well, I guess I'll go look up some St. Louis records, and see what I'm expected to do in the batting average line compared with them," the player went on. "The St. Louis team isn't a wonder, but it's done pretty fair at times, I believe, and it's a step up for me. I'll be more in line for a place on the New York Giants, or the Philadelphia Athletics if I make a good showing in Missouri," finished Joe.

He started from the room, carrying the two letters, one of which he had not yet opened.

"Who's it from?" asked Clara, with a smile, as she pointed to the heavy, square envelope in his hand.

"Oh, one of my many admirers," teased Joe. "I can't tell just which one until I open it. And, just to satisfy your curiosity, I'll do so now," and he proceeded to slit the envelope with his pocket-knife.

"Oh, it's from Mabel Varley!" he exclaimed.

"Just as if you didn't know all the while!" scoffed Clara. "You wouldn't forget her handwriting so soon, Joe Matson."

"Um!" he murmured, non-committally. "Why, this is news!" he cried, suddenly. "Mabel and her brother Reggie are coming here!"

"Here!" exclaimed Clara. "To visit us?"

"Oh, no, not that exactly," Joe went on. "They're on a trip, it seems, and they're going to stop off here for a day or so. Mabel says they'll try to see us. I hope they will."

"I've never met them," observed Clara.

"No," spoke Joe, musingly. "Well, you may soon. Why!" he went on, "they're coming to-day -- on the afternoon express. I must go down to the station to meet them, though the train is likely to be late, if this snow keeps up. Whew! see it come down!" and he went over to the window and looked out.

"It's like a small blizzard," remarked Clara, "and it seems to be growing worse. Doesn't look much like baseball; does it, Joe?"

"I should say not! Say, I believe I'll go down to the station, anyhow, and see what the prospects are. Want to come, Sis?"

"No, thank you. Not in this storm. Where are the Varleys going to stop?"

"At the hotel. Reggie has some business in town, Mabel writes. Well, I sure will be glad to see him again!"

"Him? Her, you mean!" laughed Clara. "Oh, Joe, you are so simple!"

"Humph!" he exclaimed, as he put the two letters into his pocket -- both of great importance to him. "Well, I'll go down to the station."

Joe was soon trudging through the storm on the way to the depot.

"The St. Louis Cardinals!" he mused, as he bent his head to the blast, thinking of the letters in his pocket. "I didn't think I'd be in line for a major league team so soon. I wonder if I can make good?"

Thinking alternately of the pleasure he would have in seeing Miss Mabel Varley, a girl in whom he was more than ordinarily interested, and of the new chance that had come to him, Joe soon reached the depot. His inquiries about the trains were not, however, very satisfactorily answered.

"We can't tell much about them in this storm," the station master said. "All our trains are more or less late. Stop in this afternoon, and I may have some definite information for you."

And later that day, when it was nearly arrival time for the train on which Mabel and Reggie were to come, Joe received some news that startled him.

"There's no use in your waiting, Joe," said the station master, as the young ball player approached him again. "Your train won't be in to-day, and maybe not for several days."

"Why? What's the matter -- a wreck?" cried Joe, a vision of injured friends looming before him.

"Not exactly a wreck, but almost as bad," went on the official. "The train is stalled -- snowed in at Deep Rock Cut, five miles above here, and there's no chance of getting her out."

"Great Scott!" cried Joe. "The express snowed in! Why, I've got friends on that train! I wonder what I can do to help them?"

recall_text:
Joe Matson was a pitcher for Pittston in the Central League. He was at home with his sister Clara and his mother, Mrs. Matson, whom they called “Momsey.” There was a snowy morning and the mail came. Joe was swinging his pitching arm around and he knocked a water jug out of Mrs. Matson’s hands, and then joked about it. Clara teased him about another letter that had come, one in girlish handwriting that he had not opened yet.

There was also an important letter from Mr. Gregory, the manager at Pittston. The letter said that the St. Louis Nationals, or Cardinals, were negotiating to draft Joe into the major leagues. If that happened, Joe would have to go under the baseball rules. It meant more money and fame, but also hard work and having to prove himself.

The other letter was from Mabel Varley. Mabel Varley and her brother Reggie were friends of Joe and his family, and they were coming by train and stopping in town that day. Because of that letter Joe went to the station in a snowstorm. Later he learned that their express train had been snowed in at Deep Rock Cut, about five miles away, and had been stalled there for days. Joe became worried about them and about how he could help.

"Whew!" whistled Joe Matson, the astonishment on his bronzed face being indicated by his surprised exclamation of:

"Well, what do you know about that, Sis?"

"What is it, Joe?" asked his sister Clara, as she looked up from a letter she was reading to see her brother staring at a sheet of paper he had just withdrawn from an envelope, for the morning mail had been delivered a few minutes before. "What is it?" the girl went on, laying aside her own correspondence. "Is it anything serious -- anything about father's business? Don't tell me there is more trouble, Joe!"

"I'm not going to, Clara. It isn't trouble, but, if what he says is true, it's going to make a big difference to me," and Joe looked out of the window, across a snowy expanse of yard, and gazed at, without consciously seeing, a myriad of white flakes swirling down through the wintry air.

"No, it isn't exactly trouble," went on Joe, "and I suppose I ought to be corkingly glad of it; but I hadn't counted on leaving the Central Baseball League quite so soon."

"Oh, Joe! Have you lost your place?" exclaimed Clara. "And just after you have done so well, too; and helped them win the pennant! I call that a shame! I thought baseball men were better sports than that."

"Listen to her -- my little sister using slang!" laughed Joe.

"Sports isn't slang," defended Clara. "I've heard lots of girls use it. I mean it in the right sense. But have you really lost your place on the team, Joe?"

"Well, not exactly, Sis, but I'm about to, I'm afraid. However, I guess I may as well make the best of it, and be glad. I sure can use the extra money!"

"I certainly don't know what you're talking about," went on Clara, with a helpless look at her big, handsome brother, "and I suppose you'll take your own time in telling me. But I would like to know what it all means, Joe. And about extra money. Who's going to give it to you?"

"Nobody. I'll have to earn it with this pitching arm of mine," and the young baseball player swung it around, as though "winding-up" for a swift delivery.

"Look out, Joe!" cried Clara, but she gave the warning too late.

At that moment Mrs. Matson entered the room with a jug of water, which she intended pouring on a window-box of flowers. Joe's arm struck the jug a glancing blow, and sent it flying, the water spraying over the floor, and the jug itself falling, and cracking into many pieces.

For a moment there was a momentous silence, after two startled screams -- one each from Mrs. Matson and Clara. Then Joe cried gaily:

"Out at first! Say, Momsey, I hope I didn't hit you!"

"No, you didn't," and she laughed now. "But what does it all mean? Are you practicing so early in the season? Oh, my carpet! It will be ruined!" she went on, as she saw the water. "But I'm glad I didn't bring in a good jug. Did you hurt your hand?"

"Nary a hurt," said Joe, with a smile. "Ha! I'll save you from a wetting!" he exclaimed, as he stooped quickly and picked up an unopened letter, the address of which was in a girlish hand.

"Get the mop, while you're at it," advised Clara. A little later Joe had sopped up the water, and quiet was restored.

"And now suppose you tell us all about it," suggested Mrs. Mason. "Why were you practicing gymnastics, Joe?" and she smiled at her athletic son.

"I was just telling Clara that my pitching arm was likely to bring me in more money this year, Momsey, and I was giving it a twirl, when you happened to get in my way. Now I'll tell you all about it. It's this letter," and Joe held out the one he had been reading.

"Are you sure it isn't the other?" asked Clara, with a sly look at her brother, for she had glanced at the writing on the unopened envelope Joe had picked up from the floor. "Let me read that other letter, Joe," she teased.

"A little later -- maybe!" he parried. "But this one," and he fluttered the open sheet in his hand, "this one is from Mr. Gregory, manager of the Pittston team, with whom I have the honor to be associated," and Joe bowed low to his mother and sister. "Mr. Gregory gives me a bit of news. It is nothing less than that the manager of the St. Louis Nationals is negotiating for the services of yours truly -- your humble servant, Joseph Matson," and again the young ball player bowed, and laughed.

"Joe, you don't mean it!" cried his sister. "You're going to belong to a major league team!" for Clara was almost as ardent a baseball "fan" as was her brother.

"Well, it looks like it, Sis," replied Joe, slowly, as he glanced at the letter again. "Of course it isn't settled, but Mr. Gregory says I'm pretty sure to be drafted to St. Louis."

"Drafted!" exclaimed his mother. "That sounds like war times, when they used to draft men to go to the front. Do you mean you haven't any choice in the matter, Joe?"

"Well, that's about it, Momsey," the young man explained. "You see, baseball is pretty well organized. It has to be, to make it the success it is," he added frankly, "though lots of people are opposed to the system. But I haven't been in it long enough to find fault, even if I wanted to -- which I don't."

"But it seems queer that you can't stay with the Pittston team if you want to," said Mrs. Matson.

"I don't know as I want to," spoke Joe, slowly, "especially when I'll surely get more money with St. Louis, besides having the honor of pitching for a major league team, even if it isn't one of the top-notchers, and a pennant winner. So if they want to draft me, let them do their worst!" and he laughed, showing his even, white teeth.

"You see," he resumed, "when I signed a contract with the Pittstons, of the Central League, I gave them the right to control my services as long as I played baseball. I had to agree not to go to any other team without permission, and, in fact, no other organized team would take me unless the Pittston management released me. I went into it with my eyes open.

"And, you see, the Pittston team, being one of the small ones, has to give way to a major league team. That is, any major league team, like the St. Louis Nationals, can call for, or draft, any player in a smaller team. So if they call me I'll have to go. And I'll be glad to. I'll get more money and fame.

"That is, I hope I will," and Joe spoke more soberly. "I know I'm not going to have any snap of it. It's going to be hard work from the word go, for there will be other pitchers on the St. Louis team, and I'll have to do my best to make a showing against them.

"And I will, too!" cried Joe, resolutely. "I'll make good, Momsey!"

"I hope so, my son," she responded, quietly. "You know I was not much in favor of your taking up baseball for a living, but I must say you have done well at it, and after all, if one does one's best at anything, that is what counts. So I hope you make good with the St. Louis team -- I suppose make good is the proper expression," she added, with a smile.

"It'll do first-rate, Momsey," laughed Joe. "Now let's see what else Gregory says."

He glanced over the letter again, and remarked:

"Well, there's nothing definite. The managers are laying their plans for the Spring work, and he says I'm being considered. He adds he will be sorry to lose me."

"I should think he would be!" exclaimed Clara, a flush coming into her cheeks. "You were the best pitcher on his team!"

"Oh, I wouldn't go as far as to say that!" cried Joe, "though I appreciate your feeling, Sis. I had a good bit of luck, winning some of the games the way I did. Well, I guess I'll go look up some St. Louis records, and see what I'm expected to do in the batting average line compared with them," the player went on. "The St. Louis team isn't a wonder, but it's done pretty fair at times, I believe, and it's a step up for me. I'll be more in line for a place on the New York Giants, or the Philadelphia Athletics if I make a good showing in Missouri," finished Joe.

He started from the room, carrying the two letters, one of which he had not yet opened.

"Who's it from?" asked Clara, with a smile, as she pointed to the heavy, square envelope in his hand.

"Oh, one of my many admirers," teased Joe. "I can't tell just which one until I open it. And, just to satisfy your curiosity, I'll do so now," and he proceeded to slit the envelope with his pocket-knife.

"Oh, it's from Mabel Varley!" he exclaimed.

"Just as if you didn't know all the while!" scoffed Clara. "You wouldn't forget her handwriting so soon, Joe Matson."

"Um!" he murmured, non-committally. "Why, this is news!" he cried, suddenly. "Mabel and her brother Reggie are coming here!"

"Here!" exclaimed Clara. "To visit us?"

"Oh, no, not that exactly," Joe went on. "They're on a trip, it seems, and they're going to stop off here for a day or so. Mabel says they'll try to see us. I hope they will."

"I've never met them," observed Clara.

"No," spoke Joe, musingly. "Well, you may soon. Why!" he went on, "they're coming to-day -- on the afternoon express. I must go down to the station to meet them, though the train is likely to be late, if this snow keeps up. Whew! see it come down!" and he went over to the window and looked out.

"It's like a small blizzard," remarked Clara, "and it seems to be growing worse. Doesn't look much like baseball; does it, Joe?"

"I should say not! Say, I believe I'll go down to the station, anyhow, and see what the prospects are. Want to come, Sis?"

"No, thank you. Not in this storm. Where are the Varleys going to stop?"

"At the hotel. Reggie has some business in town, Mabel writes. Well, I sure will be glad to see him again!"

"Him? Her, you mean!" laughed Clara. "Oh, Joe, you are so simple!"

"Humph!" he exclaimed, as he put the two letters into his pocket -- both of great importance to him. "Well, I'll go down to the station."

Joe was soon trudging through the storm on the way to the depot.

"The St. Louis Cardinals!" he mused, as he bent his head to the blast, thinking of the letters in his pocket. "I didn't think I'd be in line for a major league team so soon. I wonder if I can make good?"

Thinking alternately of the pleasure he would have in seeing Miss Mabel Varley, a girl in whom he was more than ordinarily interested, and of the new chance that had come to him, Joe soon reached the depot. His inquiries about the trains were not, however, very satisfactorily answered.

"We can't tell much about them in this storm," the station master said. "All our trains are more or less late. Stop in this afternoon, and I may have some definite information for you."

And later that day, when it was nearly arrival time for the train on which Mabel and Reggie were to come, Joe received some news that startled him.

"There's no use in your waiting, Joe," said the station master, as the young ball player approached him again. "Your train won't be in to-day, and maybe not for several days."

"Why? What's the matter -- a wreck?" cried Joe, a vision of injured friends looming before him.

"Not exactly a wreck, but almost as bad," went on the official. "The train is stalled -- snowed in at Deep Rock Cut, five miles above here, and there's no chance of getting her out."

"Great Scott!" cried Joe. "The express snowed in! Why, I've got friends on that train! I wonder what I can do to help them?"

"Whew!" whistled Joe Matson, the astonishment on his bronzed face being indicated by his surprised exclamation of:

"Well, what do you know about that, Sis?"

"What is it, Joe?" asked his sister Clara, as she looked up from a letter she was reading to see her brother staring at a sheet of paper he had just withdrawn from an envelope, for the morning mail had been delivered a few minutes before. "What is it?" the girl went on, laying aside her own correspondence. "Is it anything serious -- anything about father's business? Don't tell me there is more trouble, Joe!"

"I'm not going to, Clara. It isn't trouble, but, if what he says is true, it's going to make a big difference to me," and Joe looked out of the window, across a snowy expanse of yard, and gazed at, without consciously seeing, a myriad of white flakes swirling down through the wintry air.

"No, it isn't exactly trouble," went on Joe, "and I suppose I ought to be corkingly glad of it; but I hadn't counted on leaving the Central Baseball League quite so soon."

"Oh, Joe! Have you lost your place?" exclaimed Clara. "And just after you have done so well, too; and helped them win the pennant! I call that a shame! I thought baseball men were better sports than that."

"Listen to her -- my little sister using slang!" laughed Joe.

"Sports isn't slang," defended Clara. "I've heard lots of girls use it. I mean it in the right sense. But have you really lost your place on the team, Joe?"

"Well, not exactly, Sis, but I'm about to, I'm afraid. However, I guess I may as well make the best of it, and be glad. I sure can use the extra money!"

"I certainly don't know what you're talking about," went on Clara, with a helpless look at her big, handsome brother, "and I suppose you'll take your own time in telling me. But I would like to know what it all means, Joe. And about extra money. Who's going to give it to you?"

"Nobody. I'll have to earn it with this pitching arm of mine," and the young baseball player swung it around, as though "winding-up" for a swift delivery.

"Look out, Joe!" cried Clara, but she gave the warning too late.

At that moment Mrs. Matson entered the room with a jug of water, which she intended pouring on a window-box of flowers. Joe's arm struck the jug a glancing blow, and sent it flying, the water spraying over the floor, and the jug itself falling, and cracking into many pieces.

For a moment there was a momentous silence, after two startled screams -- one each from Mrs. Matson and Clara. Then Joe cried gaily:

"Out at first! Say, Momsey, I hope I didn't hit you!"

"No, you didn't," and she laughed now. "But what does it all mean? Are you practicing so early in the season? Oh, my carpet! It will be ruined!" she went on, as she saw the water. "But I'm glad I didn't bring in a good jug. Did you hurt your hand?"

"Nary a hurt," said Joe, with a smile. "Ha! I'll save you from a wetting!" he exclaimed, as he stooped quickly and picked up an unopened letter, the address of which was in a girlish hand.

"Get the mop, while you're at it," advised Clara. A little later Joe had sopped up the water, and quiet was restored.

"And now suppose you tell us all about it," suggested Mrs. Mason. "Why were you practicing gymnastics, Joe?" and she smiled at her athletic son.

"I was just telling Clara that my pitching arm was likely to bring me in more money this year, Momsey, and I was giving it a twirl, when you happened to get in my way. Now I'll tell you all about it. It's this letter," and Joe held out the one he had been reading.

"Are you sure it isn't the other?" asked Clara, with a sly look at her brother, for she had glanced at the writing on the unopened envelope Joe had picked up from the floor. "Let me read that other letter, Joe," she teased.

"A little later -- maybe!" he parried. "But this one," and he fluttered the open sheet in his hand, "this one is from Mr. Gregory, manager of the Pittston team, with whom I have the honor to be associated," and Joe bowed low to his mother and sister. "Mr. Gregory gives me a bit of news. It is nothing less than that the manager of the St. Louis Nationals is negotiating for the services of yours truly -- your humble servant, Joseph Matson," and again the young ball player bowed, and laughed.

"Joe, you don't mean it!" cried his sister. "You're going to belong to a major league team!" for Clara was almost as ardent a baseball "fan" as was her brother.

"Well, it looks like it, Sis," replied Joe, slowly, as he glanced at the letter again. "Of course it isn't settled, but Mr. Gregory says I'm pretty sure to be drafted to St. Louis."

"Drafted!" exclaimed his mother. "That sounds like war times, when they used to draft men to go to the front. Do you mean you haven't any choice in the matter, Joe?"

"Well, that's about it, Momsey," the young man explained. "You see, baseball is pretty well organized. It has to be, to make it the success it is," he added frankly, "though lots of people are opposed to the system. But I haven't been in it long enough to find fault, even if I wanted to -- which I don't."

"But it seems queer that you can't stay with the Pittston team if you want to," said Mrs. Matson.

"I don't know as I want to," spoke Joe, slowly, "especially when I'll surely get more money with St. Louis, besides having the honor of pitching for a major league team, even if it isn't one of the top-notchers, and a pennant winner. So if they want to draft me, let them do their worst!" and he laughed, showing his even, white teeth.

"You see," he resumed, "when I signed a contract with the Pittstons, of the Central League, I gave them the right to control my services as long as I played baseball. I had to agree not to go to any other team without permission, and, in fact, no other organized team would take me unless the Pittston management released me. I went into it with my eyes open.

"And, you see, the Pittston team, being one of the small ones, has to give way to a major league team. That is, any major league team, like the St. Louis Nationals, can call for, or draft, any player in a smaller team. So if they call me I'll have to go. And I'll be glad to. I'll get more money and fame.

"That is, I hope I will," and Joe spoke more soberly. "I know I'm not going to have any snap of it. It's going to be hard work from the word go, for there will be other pitchers on the St. Louis team, and I'll have to do my best to make a showing against them.

"I hope so, my son," she responded, quietly. "Him? Her, you mean!" laughed Clara. "Oh, Joe, you are so simple!"

One snowy morning the mail came and there was a letter from Mr. Gregory. The letter said that the St. Louis Nationals, or Cardinals, were negotiating to draft Joe from Pittston into the major leagues. It meant more money and fame, though nothing was definite yet.

At home Joe was excited and swinging his pitching arm around. He knocked over and broke Mrs. Matson’s water jug, and joked about it before explaining what was in the letter.

Mabel and Reggie were due on the afternoon express during the snowstorm. Joe went to the station, but learned that the train had been snowed in at Deep Rock Cut, about five miles away. It might be stuck there for days, and Joe was worried because his friends were on board.

Joe got a letter from Mr. Gregory, the Pittston manager, saying that the St. Louis Nationals, or Cardinals, were negotiating to draft him into the major leagues. It meant more money for Joe, but he would have to prove himself against other pitchers.

While they were excitedly talking about it at home, Joe swung his pitching arm and knocked a jug out of Mrs. Matson’s hand. The water spilled and the jug broke. Joe joked about it and cleaned up the mess, and Clara teased him about another letter that had not been opened.

Mabel and Reggie were coming on the afternoon express during a snowstorm. Joe went to the depot to meet them. Later the station master said that the train was stalled and snowed in at Deep Rock Cut, five miles away, and that it would not arrive that day.

recall_text:
I grew up in Providence, Rhode Island, in an Irish Catholic family that was obsessed with the Kennedys. The tragedy of JFK felt to my family like a family tragedy. My father once pulled over on I-95 when my sister Erin said Mikayla was crying about JFK, and with tears in his eyes he said, “don’t you ever be ashamed to cry for that man.”

In the seventies we took vacations in a rented beach house in Hyannis, near the Kennedy compound, with my four aunts and two cousins. My aunts spent whole days spying on the Kennedys with binoculars and talking about Rose, Ethel, Bobby, and Jackie. Aunt Pat usually made the first sightings. Aunt Gurt would ask how old they were, and Aunt Momo would calculate and then say it in a Kennedy-esque voice.

When I was nine, my cousins and I drifted out to sea in a tiny half-inflated boat. We had no oars and no life vests. David and Michael Kennedy rescued us in a power boat. My aunts were furious, mostly because the Kennedys had to save us, as if it were going to become another Kennedy tragedy.

After that I was punished and had to stay in the shallow water. We played chicken fights, and I accidentally kicked Uncle Al in the head. His expensive magnetized fake eye popped out and sank. Everybody panicked and searched for it, and my cousin Kevin finally found it. Uncle Al rinsed it off and popped it back in. Later this became one of the family stories, and I realized that David and Michael Kennedy had seen the whole thing with Uncle Al’s eye.

hi. i grew up in providence rhode island, and for my entire childhood we were never more than twenty miles away from the core of our universe, the kennedys. We were irish; they were irish. We were catholic; they were catholic. They were family. We were like the relatives that they never got to see, but we knew you know they're busy and we knew that they loved us. so anything, so anything that was happening to them was also happening to us. So their tragedy plus our own tragedy was a lot. So this one thanksgiving after dinner and a family fight at grandma's house, um we were in the car and were driving home and the radio was playing this tenth uh anniversary of the jfk assassination. and i'm sitting in the back seat and i start to cry. and my sister erin says, "hey dad, mikayla's crying." And my father pulls that car right over to the shoulder of I95. He stops it. He turns around and he looks at us, and with tears in his own eyes he says, "don't you ever be ashamed to cry for that man." So my parents grew up near newport and they got married in the same exact church as jack and jackie saint mary's. And my father gave exact replica jewelry to my mother that was replications of the jewelry that jack gave to jackie. And every saturday night after mass, my family would be in the living room and we'd be happily ever aftering to the original soundtrack of camelot. And every year during the seventies my four aunts would take me and my two cousins on their dream vacation, a rented beach house in hyannis on the very cove sharing beachfront with the kennedy compound. Every day for an entire week, my aunt pat would roll up her sisters' hair. My aunts would apply sunscreen to the back of their necks, the backs of the hands, and the tops of their feet, and then they would drag their beach chairs down to the beach. And they would set them up perfectly, not facing the water, not into the sun for tanning, but perfectly for spying on the kennedys. They would sit there all day in the broiling sun with high powered binoculars, and keep a constant surveillance. And every year they'd have the same exact conversations, usually around mid morning. The first sighting would be made usually by my aunt pat. She'd be, "ah, they got rose out walking. ethel looks drawn." And then about an hour later my aunt gurt would say, "how old is rose now?" and aunt momo would make the calculations, "well let's see.  jack died in sixty three when she was seventy four, and rose's birthday was two weeks last thursday, and joe died in sixty nine making her a widow at eighty one. so eighty five." and then they'd break for lunch. So after lobster and drawn butter and hosing us down, they'd all huffle back to their posts, and they'd watch. And every now and then there'd be something they didn't know, "hey, who's that? who's that? who's that?" So they draw out the family tree in the sand. They'd analyze it; they'd come up with a profile and they'd crack the code: "It's one of bobby's." Now any mention of bobby would always bring up the inevitable, "oh, i just pray to god they don't tell poor senile rose about bobby. it'll break her." I grew up in Providence, Rhode Island, in an Irish Catholic family that was obsessed with the Kennedys. Grief over JFK felt like family grief. Once, on an anniversary of JFK, I was crying in the car on I-95, and my father pulled over and told me never to be ashamed to cry for that man.

In the seventies we took beach vacations in Hyannis with four aunts and two cousins, beside the Kennedy compound. My aunts spent whole days spying with binoculars and talking about Rose, Ethel, Bobby, Jackie, and making the family tree in the sand.

When I was nine, my cousins and I drifted out to sea in a tiny half-inflated boat with no oars or life vests. David and Michael Kennedy came in a power boat and rescued us. My aunts seemed more upset that the Kennedys had to save us than that we were in danger.

After that I was punished and had to stay in the shallow water. We played chicken fights, and I accidentally kicked Uncle Al in the head. His expensive magnetized fake eye popped out and sank. Everybody searched frantically until my cousin Kevin found it. Uncle Al rinsed it off and popped it back in. At the end I noticed that David and Michael Kennedy had watched the whole fake-eye episode.

I grew up in Providence, Rhode Island, in an Irish Catholic family that felt deeply tied to the Kennedys, as if their joys and tragedies were our family’s too. My father once pulled over on I-95 when my sister Erin said Mikayla was crying during a JFK assassination anniversary radio show, and with tears he said, “don’t you ever be ashamed to cry for that man.”

Our Kennedy obsession centered on Hyannis beach vacations beside the Kennedy compound. My four aunts—Pat, Gurt, Momo, and another aunt—sat all day with binoculars spying and talking about Rose, Ethel, Bobby, Jackie, and making family-tree guesses in the sand.

When I was nine, my cousins Ilene and Kevin and I drifted out to sea in a tiny half-inflated boat with no oars or life vests. David and Michael Kennedy rescued us in a power boat. recall_text:
I grew up in Providence, Rhode Island, in an Irish Catholic family that was obsessed with the Kennedys. In my family, the JFK tragedy felt like a family tragedy. Once, on an anniversary of JFK’s death, I was crying in the car on I-95, and my father pulled over and told me never to be ashamed to cry for that man.

In the seventies we took vacations in Hyannis, near the Kennedy compound, with my four aunts—Pat, Gurt, Momo, and another aunt—and two cousins. My aunts would spend whole days spying on the Kennedys with binoculars. They talked constantly about Rose, Ethel, Bobby, Jackie, and made the family tree in the sand.

When I was nine, my cousins and I drifted out to sea in a tiny half-inflated boat. We had no oars and no life vests. David and Michael Kennedy came out in a power boat and rescued us. My aunts were furious, but because the Kennedys had saved us they acted polite. After that, our punishment was that we could stay only on the beach or in the water up to our knees.

Another time, during chicken fights in the shallow water, I accidentally kicked Uncle Al’s fake eye out. It was magnetized. Everybody panicked and blamed me while they searched for it. My cousin Kevin finally found the eye, and Uncle Al rinsed it off and popped it back in. Later my family kept retelling that story, and I realized that David and Michael Kennedy had witnessed the whole thing.

recall_text:
I grew up in Providence, Rhode Island, in an Irish Catholic family that was obsessed with the Kennedys. In my family, grief over JFK felt like family grief. I remember crying on an anniversary of JFK’s death while we were on I-95, and my father stopped the car and told me never to be ashamed to cry for that man.

In the seventies we took Hyannis beach vacations with my four aunts and two cousins, near the Kennedy compound. My aunts spent their days spying with binoculars and talking about Rose, Ethel, Bobby, Jackie, and the Kennedy family tree instead of watching the kids.

When I was nine, my cousins and I drifted out to sea in a tiny half-inflated boat with no oars or life vests. David and Michael Kennedy came out in a power boat and rescued us. My aunts were more upset that the Kennedys had to save us than they were about the fact that we had been in danger.

After that, as punishment, we had to stay in the shallow water. We played chicken fights, and I accidentally kicked Uncle Al in the head. His expensive magnetized fake eye popped out and sank. Everybody searched frantically for it until my cousin Kevin found it. Uncle Al rinsed it off and popped it back in.

recall_text:
I grew up in Providence, Rhode Island, in an Irish Catholic family that was obsessed with the Kennedys. In my family, grief over JFK felt personal. Once my father pulled over on I-95 when my sister Erin said I was crying during a JFK anniversary program on the radio, and he said, “don’t you ever be ashamed to cry for that man.”

In the seventies we took vacations in Hyannis with four aunts and two cousins, staying at a beach house by the Kennedy compound. My aunts sat all day with binoculars spying on the Kennedys and talking about Rose, Ethel, Bobby, and Jackie. Aunt Pat usually made the first sightings, Aunt Gurt asked how old everyone was, and Aunt Momo did the calculations and spoke in a fake Kennedy voice.

When I was nine, my cousins and I drifted out to sea in a tiny half-inflated boat with no oars and no life vests. David and Michael Kennedy came out in a power boat and rescued us. My aunts were furious, but because the Kennedys had saved us they acted polite. They were especially upset that the Kennedys had to deal with our near-drowning.

After that, I was punished and had to stay in the shallow water. We played chicken fights, and I accidentally kicked Uncle Al in the head. His expensive magnetized fake eye popped out and sank. Everyone panicked and blamed me. After a search, my cousin Kevin found the eye, Uncle Al rinsed it off and popped it back in, and later I realized that David and Michael Kennedy had seen the whole thing.

In the summers in Hyannis on the Cape, my four aunts took me and my two cousins to a rented beach house by the Kennedy compound. We spent days spying with binoculars and talking about Rose, Ethel, Jackie, and the Kennedy family tree.

I grew up in Providence, Rhode Island, in an Irish Catholic family that was obsessed with the Kennedys. In my family, grief over John F. Kennedy felt almost like grief for one of our own.

I remember one time after Thanksgiving, after some kind of family fight, I was crying in the car when something about the anniversary of JFK’s assassination came on the radio. My father pulled over on I-95 and, with tears in his eyes, told me, “don’t you ever be ashamed to cry for that man.”

In the 1970s, four of my aunts took me and my cousins, Ilene and Kevin, to Hyannis. We rented a place near the Kennedy compound. My aunts spent days spying on the Kennedys with binoculars and gossiping about Rose, Ethel, Jackie, and Bobby’s children.

When I was nine, my cousins and I drifted out to sea in a tiny half-inflated boat and were rescued by David and Michael Kennedy. Later, during chicken fights, I kicked Uncle Al in the head and his expensive magnetized fake eye popped out and sank. It was found and put back in, and after that my family kept retelling the story.

recall_text:
I grew up in Providence, Rhode Island, in an Irish Catholic family that was obsessed with the Kennedys. We felt their joys and tragedies as if they were family.

When I was a child, after Thanksgiving, I heard on the radio about the anniversary of JFK’s assassination and I cried. My sister Erin told my dad, and he pulled over on I-95 and, with tears in his eyes, said, “don’t you ever be ashamed to cry for that man.”

In the 1970s, four of my aunts took me and my cousins, Ilene and Kevin, to a beach house in Hyannis near the Kennedy compound. We spent our days spying with binoculars and talking about Rose, Ethel, Jackie, and one of Bobby’s.

When I was nine, we drifted out in a tiny boat and were rescued by David and Michael Kennedy. Later, when I was being punished with limited swimming, I kicked Uncle Al’s hidden fake magnetized eye out and it sank. Kevin found it, and David and Michael had seen it happen.

I remember once crying on an anniversary of JFK’s death while we were on I-95, and my father pulled over and told me never to be ashamed to cry for that man.

In the seventies we took vacations in Hyannis, near the Kennedy compound, with my four aunts—Pat, Gurt, Momo, and another aunt—and two cousins. My aunts spent their days spying on the Kennedys with binoculars and talking about Rose, Ethel, Bobby, and Jackie.

When I was nine, my cousins and I drifted out to sea in a tiny half-inflated boat with no oars or life vests. David and Michael Kennedy came out in a power boat and rescued us. My aunts were furious, mostly because the Kennedys had to save us.

As punishment we were told to stay in the shallow water, and we played chicken fights. I accidentally kicked Uncle Al’s fake eye out. It was magnetized, and everybody panicked because of how much it would cost. The family searched the water until my cousin Kevin found it. Uncle Al rinsed it off and popped it back in.

Later my family kept retelling the story, and apparently David and Michael Kennedy had witnessed the whole fake-eye episode too.

I grew up in Providence, Rhode Island, in an Irish Catholic family that was obsessed with the Kennedys. The JFK tragedy felt like a family tragedy to us. Once, on an anniversary of JFK’s death, I was crying in the car on I-95, and my father pulled over and told me never to be ashamed to cry for that man.

Every summer in the 1970s, my four aunts took me and my cousins, Ilene and Kevin, to a rented beach house in Hyannis, near the Kennedy compound. We spent our days spying with binoculars and talking about Rose, Ethel, Jackie, and Bobby’s children.

When I was nine, my cousins and I drifted out to sea in a tiny half-inflated boat. We had no oars and no life vests. David and Michael Kennedy came out in a power boat and rescued us. My aunts were furious, mostly because the Kennedys had to save us.

Later, when we were being punished with limited swimming, I accidentally kicked Uncle Al in the head during chicken fights, and his expensive magnetized fake eye popped out and sank. Everybody searched frantically, and then my cousin Kevin found it. Uncle Al rinsed it off and popped it back in. At the end I realized that David and Michael Kennedy had watched the whole thing with the eye.

I grew up in Providence, Rhode Island, in an Irish Catholic family that was obsessed with the Kennedys. In my family, the tragedy of JFK felt like a family tragedy. I remember crying over a JFK anniversary, and my father pulled over on I-95 and told me never to be ashamed to cry for that man.

In the seventies we took vacations in Hyannis, near the Kennedy compound, with my four aunts—Pat, Gurt, Momo, and another aunt—and two cousins. My aunts spent whole days spying on the Kennedys with binoculars and talking about Rose, Ethel, Bobby, and Jackie.

When I was nine, my cousins and I drifted out to sea in a tiny half-inflated boat. We had no oars and no life vests. David and Michael Kennedy came and rescued us in a power boat. My aunts were furious, but because the Kennedys had saved us they acted polite.

After that I was punished and told to stay in the shallow water. During chicken fights, I accidentally kicked Uncle Al’s fake eye out. It was magnetized. Everybody panicked and searched the water for it until my cousin Kevin found it. Uncle Al popped it back in, and after that my family kept retelling the story.

recall_text:
I grew up in Providence, Rhode Island, in an Irish Catholic family that was obsessed with the Kennedys. In my family, grief over JFK felt like family grief. I remember once crying on the anniversary of JFK’s death while we were on I-95, and my father pulled over and told me never to be ashamed to cry for that man.

In the seventies we took Hyannis beach vacations near the Kennedy compound with my four aunts—Pat, Gurt, Momo, and another aunt. They spent the whole day spying with binoculars and talking about Rose, Ethel, Bobby, and Jackie. Their beach chairs faced the compound instead of the water.

When I was nine, my cousins and I drifted out to sea in a tiny half-inflated boat. We had no oars and no life vests. David and Michael Kennedy came out in a power boat and rescued us. My aunts were furious, mostly because the Kennedys had to save us.

Later, during chicken fights in shallow water, I kicked Uncle Al in the head and his expensive magnetized fake eye popped out and sank. Everybody panicked and searched for it. My cousin Kevin finally found it, and Uncle Al rinsed it off and popped it back in. David and Michael Kennedy had apparently seen the whole thing.

I’m Mikayla, and I grew up in Providence, Rhode Island, in an Irish Catholic family that was obsessed with the Kennedys. When JFK was killed, my family felt the grief almost like it was a death in the family. I remember my father pulling over on I-95, crying, and telling me, “don’t you ever be ashamed to cry for that man.”

In the 1970s, my four aunts took me and my cousins, Ilene and Kevin, to a rented beach house in Hyannis near the Kennedy compound. The aunts spent their days spying on the Kennedys with binoculars and gossiping about Rose, Ethel, Jackie, and Bobby’s children.

When I was nine, my cousins and I drifted out to sea in a tiny half-inflated boat. We had no oars and no life vests. We were rescued by David and Michael Kennedy, which horrified my aunts, though they also acted starstruck and fake polite.

After that, we were punished and told to stay in the shallow water. We played chicken fights, and I accidentally kicked Uncle Al in the head. His expensive magnetized fake eye popped out and sank. Everybody searched frantically until my cousin Kevin found it, and Uncle Al rinsed it off and popped it back in.

When I was nine, my cousins and I drifted out to sea in a tiny half-inflated boat with no oars or life vests. David and Michael Kennedy rescued us in a power boat. My aunts were furious, mostly because the Kennedys had to save us.

I grew up in Providence, Rhode Island, in an Irish Catholic family that was obsessed with the Kennedys. In my family, grief over JFK felt like family grief. I remember crying on an anniversary of JFK’s death, and my father pulled over on I-95 and told me never to be ashamed to cry for that man.

In the seventies we took vacations in Hyannis, near the Kennedy compound, with four aunts—Pat, Gurt, Momo, and another aunt—and two cousins. My aunts spent days spying on the Kennedys with binoculars and talking about Rose, Ethel, Jackie, and Bobby’s children.

When I was nine, my cousins and I drifted out to sea in a tiny half-inflated boat with no oars or life vests. David and Michael Kennedy rescued us in a power boat. My aunts were more upset that the Kennedys had to save us than they were about the danger we had been in.

Later, when our swimming was limited as punishment and we were doing chicken fights, I accidentally kicked Uncle Al in the head and his expensive magnetized fake eye popped out and sank. Everyone panicked and searched for it, and then my cousin Kevin found it. Uncle Al rinsed it off and popped it back in.

I grew up in Providence, Rhode Island, in an Irish Catholic family that was obsessed with the Kennedys. Grief over JFK felt like family grief to us. I remember crying on an anniversary of JFK’s death, and my father pulled over on I-95 and told me never to be ashamed to cry for that man.

In the seventies we took beach vacations in Hyannis with four aunts and two cousins. We would spy on the Kennedy compound with binoculars. There was always talk about Rose, Ethel, Jackie, Bobby, and people would draw or discuss the family tree in the sand.

When I was nine, my cousins and I drifted out to sea in a tiny half-inflated boat with no oars and no life vests. David and Michael Kennedy came out in a power boat and rescued us. My aunts were furious, but because the Kennedys were there they acted polite.

After that I was punished and told to stay in the shallow water. During chicken fights Uncle Al joined in, and I kicked him in the head. His expensive magnetized fake eye popped out and sank. Everybody panicked and searched for it until my cousin Kevin found it. Uncle Al rinsed it off and popped it back in. Later I realized that David and Michael Kennedy had seen the whole fake-eye episode.

I grew up in Providence, Rhode Island, in an Irish Catholic family that was obsessed with the Kennedys. The grief over JFK felt like family grief. My father once pulled over on I-95 and said, “don’t you ever be ashamed to cry for that man.”

In the seventies we took Hyannis beach vacations with four aunts—Pat, Gurt, Momo, and another aunt—and two cousins. My aunts spent days spying on the Kennedy compound with binoculars and talking about Rose, Ethel, Jackie, and “one of Bobby’s.”

I grew up in Providence, Rhode Island, in an Irish Catholic family that was obsessed with the Kennedys. In my family, grief over JFK felt like family grief. My father once pulled over on I-95 when I cried on a JFK anniversary, and he told me never to be ashamed to cry for that man.

In the 1970s, four of my aunts took me and my cousins, Ilene and Kevin, to a rented beach house in Hyannis near the Kennedy compound. We spent our days spying on the Kennedys with binoculars and gossiping about Rose, Ethel, Jackie, and Bobby’s children.

When I was nine, my cousins and I drifted out to sea in a tiny half-inflated boat with no oars or life vests. We were rescued by David and Michael Kennedy. My aunts were furious, mostly because the Kennedys had to save us.

As punishment we had to stay in the shallow water, where we played chicken fights. I accidentally kicked Uncle Al in the head and his expensive magnetized fake eye popped out and sank. Everyone searched frantically until my cousin Kevin found it. Uncle Al rinsed it off and popped it back in. After that, my family immediately began retelling the story, and I noticed that David and Michael Kennedy had seen the whole thing.

recall_text:
I grew up in Providence, Rhode Island, in an Irish Catholic family that was obsessed with the Kennedys. Grief over JFK felt like family grief. My father once pulled over on I-95 when I was crying over a JFK anniversary and told me never to be ashamed to cry for that man.

In the seventies we took vacations in Hyannis, near the Kennedy compound, with my four aunts—Pat, Gurt, Momo, and another aunt. They spent all day spying with binoculars and constantly talking about Rose, Ethel, Bobby, and Jackie. They ignored us kids in the water.

When I was nine, my cousins Ilene and Kevin and I drifted out to sea in a tiny half-inflated boat with no oars or life vests. David and Michael Kennedy rescued us in a power boat. My aunts were furious, mostly because the Kennedys had to save us.

Later, while we were being punished or had limited swimming, we were doing chicken fights and I kicked Uncle Al in the head. His expensive magnetized fake eye popped out and sank. Everybody panicked and searched for it, and Kevin found it. Uncle Al rinsed it off and popped it back in. At the end, David and Michael Kennedy had apparently seen the whole fake-eye episode.
